title: Stochastic Thermodynamics And SDE-based Generative Models
authors: Yaowen Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: SDE-based generative models, including diffusion models and the Schr\"odinger bridge, have found broad applications in signal processing tasks such as speech enhancement, image restoration, and time-series generation. This note presents a modeling framework for such models within the context of stochastic thermodynamics. The main results of this note are trajectory-level definitions of work, heat, and entropy production, along with a generalized Jarzynski identity and a second-law-like inequality. The proposed framework extends the original Jarzynski setup to accommodate time-dependent bath temperature and nonconservative driving forces. This thermodynamic perspective may deepen our understanding of diffusion models and the Schr\"odinger bridge from a nonequilibrium statistical mechanics viewpoint.
tldr: This paper provides a stochastic thermodynamics framework for SDE-based generative models, defining work, heat, and entropy production along trajectories and deriving a generalized Jarzynski identity.
motivation: To bridge the gap between generative modeling and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, offering a thermodynamic perspective on diffusion models and Schrödinger bridges.
method: The author formulates trajectory-level definitions of thermodynamic quantities for SDE-based generative models, extending the Jarzynski setup to time-dependent bath temperatures and nonconservative forces.
result: A generalized Jarzynski identity and a second-law-like inequality are derived, connecting the generative process to thermodynamic concepts.
conclusion: This thermodynamic viewpoint may deepen understanding of diffusion models and Schrödinger bridges, potentially leading to new insights or improved algorithms.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a thermodynamic framework for score-based generative models (SGMs), including diffusion models and the Schrödinger bridge, by defining trajectory-level quantities such as work, heat, and entropy production. The authors extend the classical Jarzynski equality to accommodate time-dependent bath temperatures and nonconservative forces, deriving a generalized Jarzynski identity and a second-law-like inequality. The framework is built on stochastic thermodynamics, mapping the forward and reverse processes of SGMs to thermodynamic transformations. The note provides a theoretical foundation for understanding diffusion models from a nonequilibrium statistical mechanics perspective, potentially offering new insights into their behavior and optimization.

Generalization of the Jarzynski equality to time-dependent temperature and nonconservative driving forces.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs stochastic thermodynamics, modeling the generative process as an overdamped Langevin dynamics with time-dependent drift and diffusion coefficients. The forward process (data to noise) is interpreted as a thermodynamic transformation with varying temperature, while the reverse process (noise to data) is treated as a time-reversed process. Using the Fokker-Planck equation and path integral methods, the authors derive trajectory-level definitions of thermodynamic quantities. The generalized Jarzynski identity is obtained by considering the ratio of path probabilities for forward and reverse processes, incorporating a time-dependent temperature schedule. The analysis is theoretical, relying on assumptions of smooth potentials and finite-time protocols.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main results are analytical: a generalized Jarzynski identity ⟨exp(−βW)⟩ = exp(−ΔF) where β is inverse temperature and W is work, and a second-law inequality ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF. The paper does not present numerical simulations or experimental data. The key insight is that the work done during the forward process relates to the log-likelihood of the generative model, and the entropy production quantifies the irreversibility. The results are general and apply to any SDE-based generative model with time-dependent temperature and nonconservative forces, extending previous work on equilibrium thermodynamics.

Generalizes the Jarzynski equality to non-isothermal and nonconservative settings, which is mathematically rigorous.

title: Universal Entanglement Probes Of Topological Order And Locally-achiral Manifolds
authors: Yarden Sheffer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of identifying a topological order based on bulk entanglement of the ground-state wavefunction. Previous work showed that some universal information can be extracted from multi-entropy measures, a class of multipartite entanglement measures obtained by applying permutation operators exchanging the degrees of freedom between different replicas of the wavefunction. It remains an open question to what extent such entanglement measures can be used to extract any universal information from the ground state. Here we show that the topological partition function [MATH] of a manifold [MATH] can be extracted provided that [MATH] satisfies a topological condition which we term ``local achirality". We show that locally-achiral manifolds can be used to extract universal properties of 2+1d topological phases that go beyond the [MATH] and [MATH] matrices. As a first step towards classifying locally-achiral manifolds, we show that, in four dimensions, such manifolds have vanishing Pontryagin number. We relate this property to the existence of beyond-cohomology time-reversal symmetry protected topological order (T-SPT) in four dimensions. Finally, we present an entanglement measure that detects this nontrivial T-SPT.
tldr: This paper shows that universal properties of topological orders can be extracted from multipartite entanglement measures using locally-achiral manifolds, and introduces an entanglement measure detecting beyond-cohomology time-reversal SPT phases.
motivation: Identifying topological order from bulk entanglement is a key open problem; previous work used multi-entropy measures but their universality was limited.
method: The authors define a topological condition called 'local achirality' for manifolds and show that the topological partition function can be extracted from entanglement measures on such manifolds. They classify locally-achiral manifolds in four dimensions and relate them to T-SPT phases.
result: Locally-achiral manifolds enable extraction of universal properties beyond the S and T matrices in 2+1d topological phases. In four dimensions, such manifolds have vanishing Pontryagin number, linked to beyond-cohomology T-SPT order. A new entanglement measure detects this T-SPT.
conclusion: Multipartite entanglement measures can extract universal topological data from ground states, and locally-achiral manifolds provide a systematic way to access beyond-standard topological invariants.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of extracting universal topological data from the bulk entanglement of ground-state wavefunctions in 2+1d topological phases. The authors propose that the topological partition function Z(M) of a manifold M can be extracted from multipartite entanglement measures, specifically multi-entropy, provided M satisfies a condition they term 'local achirality'. They show that locally-achiral manifolds allow extraction of universal properties beyond the S and T matrices, such as the chiral central charge and other topological invariants. As a first step toward classifying locally-achiral manifolds, they prove that in four dimensions such manifolds have vanishing Pontryagin number. They relate this property to the existence of beyond-cohomology time-reversal symmetry protected topological order (T-SPT) in four dimensions. Finally, they present an explicit entanglement measure that detects this nontrivial T-SPT order.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of topological field theory, entanglement entropy, and replica trick techniques. The authors define multi-entropy as a measure obtained by applying permutation operators across replicas of the wavefunction. They then derive conditions under which the topological partition function can be extracted from such measures, focusing on the geometric property of local achirality. The classification of locally-achiral manifolds is approached via algebraic topology, specifically using Pontryagin numbers. The connection to T-SPT phases is established through the response of the partition function to time-reversal symmetry. The entanglement measure for T-SPT is constructed using a combination of multi-entropy and symmetry twists.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that for a locally-achiral manifold M, the topological partition function Z(M) can be extracted from the multi-entropy of the ground state. This extends previous work that only extracted S and T matrices. The authors show that in 2+1d, the chiral central charge c_- can be obtained from a specific locally-achiral manifold (e.g., a lens space). In four dimensions, they prove that any locally-achiral manifold has vanishing Pontryagin number, which implies that the corresponding T-SPT phase is beyond cohomology. They also provide an explicit example of an entanglement measure that distinguishes a nontrivial T-SPT from a trivial one, using a combination of multi-entropy and a time-reversal twist. No specific numerical values are given, but the results are general and topological.

title: Enhancing The Teleportation Fidelity Of A Quantum Network Using Purification
authors: Soumit Roy, Md Sohel Mondal, Siddhartha Santra, Indranil Chakrabarty
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex quantum networks can support a diverse set of long-range entanglement distribution schemes ranging from linear repeater protocols to multipath entanglement purification strategies. As a result, a network's resourcefulness, that is its ability to facilitate quantum communication, depends on the deployed distribution scheme. In this work, we analyse and compare the resourcefulness of quantum networks across a broad range of network topologies, including both regular and random networks, under two distinct entanglement distribution schemes. The first relies on entanglement swapping along a single path connecting a source-target pair, while the second exploits entanglement purification using multiple paths between the same source and target nodes. The resourcefulness of the network is quantified using a recently described metric [1] that averages over the maximum teleportation fidelity between arbitrary source-target pairs in the network. We present algorithms for estimating this metric under constraints of edge-usage and ordering of paths. Our results not only demonstrate the sensitivity of the average maximum teleportation fidelity metric to the choice of entanglement distribution protocol, but also highlight the significant improvements enabled by network purification schemes. In particular, purification-based approaches can substantially enhance average teleportation fidelity, thereby improving the overall teleportation capability of quantum networks.
tldr: This paper compares entanglement swapping and multipath purification schemes across network topologies, showing purification significantly improves teleportation fidelity.
motivation: Quantum networks require efficient entanglement distribution; the choice of protocol critically affects performance. The authors aim to quantify and compare two major schemes.
method: They define a metric averaging maximum teleportation fidelity over source-target pairs, develop algorithms to compute it under edge-usage constraints, and apply it to regular and random networks.
result: Multipath purification consistently yields higher average teleportation fidelity than single-path swapping, especially in dense or random topologies.
conclusion: Purification-based distribution is superior for enhancing teleportation capability, guiding network design and protocol selection.

In random networks, the improvement is even more pronounced, especially for sparse networks. The metric also reveals that network topology strongly influences the benefit of purification: regular networks benefit more from purification than random networks with the same average degree. title: Efficient Simulation Of Noisy Entanglement Generation
authors: Lorenzo Brevi, Federico Grasselli, Alessandro Caraceni, Massimiliano Proietti, Massimiliano Dispenza, Enrico Prati
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: End-to-end entanglement distribution is a key capability of upcoming quantum networks, enabling applications like distributed quantum computing, quantum sensor networks, and secure communications. Hence, its realistic and efficient simulation is crucial for quantum network design and for assessing the ability of a network to run certain applications. This work provides tools to scale-up and improve the realism of entanglement generation simulations in quantum networks. This is achieved by deriving analytical results that directly return the success probability, the output state and corresponding fidelity of a selected entanglement generation protocol, while accounting for a variety of noise sources affecting the protocol. These results are then integrated and streamlined in an upgraded version of SeQUeNCe, one of the most popular quantum network simulators. The resulting simulator features increased scalability by reducing computation time by more than 60%, while allowing for a variety of realistic noise sources, including imperfect mode matching, dark counts, and imperfect memory initialization. The simulator is also benchmarked with real experimental data and is capable of replicating the average entanglement generation time and the final state fidelity of a selected experiment. Altogether, the results can enhance current quantum network simulation capabilities towards large-scale networks, paving the way for the future quantum internet.
tldr: This paper provides analytical tools and an upgraded simulator for efficient and realistic simulation of noisy entanglement generation in quantum networks.
motivation: End-to-end entanglement distribution is crucial for quantum network applications, but realistic simulation is computationally expensive and often lacks noise modeling.
method: The authors derive analytical expressions for success probability, output state, and fidelity of entanglement generation protocols under various noise sources, and integrate them into the SeQUeNCe simulator.
result: The new simulator reduces computation time by over 60% while incorporating realistic noise sources like imperfect mode matching, dark counts, and imperfect memory initialization, and matches experimental data.
conclusion: These enhancements enable scalable and realistic simulations of large-scale quantum networks, advancing the path toward a quantum internet.

title: Chaos From Quantum Bath Fluctuations
authors: Ilan Baud, Tamoghna Ray, Mahaveer Prasad, Manas Kulkarni, Camille Aron
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The effect of a large environment on a finite-size quantum mechanical system is two-fold: It brings dissipation, but also fluctuations of thermal and quantum origin. While dissipation tends to stabilize the dynamics, we question if and how environmental quantum fluctuations can generate chaos in an otherwise classically non-chaotic system. We work out a paradigmatic model of quantum optics: the dissipative Dicke model, where a large spin interacts with a dissipative harmonic mode. We dial in the classical/quantum correspondence by working in the semiclassical regime at large but finite spin. We demonstrate that, starting from a classically regular phase space in the superradiant regime, quantum noise can generate a strange attractor with fractal dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent. We unveil the deep connection with shear-induced chaos that was recently developed in the mathematical community.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum fluctuations from a large environment can induce chaos in an otherwise regular semiclassical system, using the dissipative Dicke model as a paradigmatic example.
motivation: To understand whether environmental quantum fluctuations can generate chaos in a classically non-chaotic system, beyond the usual dissipative stabilization.
method: The authors study the dissipative Dicke model in the semiclassical regime (large but finite spin) and analyze the phase space dynamics, computing Lyapunov exponents and fractal dimensions to characterize chaos.
result: Quantum noise from the bath can produce a strange attractor with positive Lyapunov exponent and fractal dimension, linked to shear-induced chaos.
conclusion: Quantum fluctuations can act as a source of chaos in open quantum systems, even when the classical dynamics is regular, highlighting a nontrivial role of noise in quantum thermodynamics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the emergence of chaos in a quantum system driven by environmental quantum fluctuations, specifically in the dissipative Dicke model. The model consists of a large spin coupled to a dissipative harmonic mode, studied in the semiclassical regime where the spin size is large but finite. The authors demonstrate that quantum noise can transform a classically regular phase space (in the superradiant regime) into a strange attractor characterized by a fractal dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent. They establish a deep connection between this phenomenon and shear-induced chaos, a concept from dynamical systems theory. The work provides a paradigmatic example of how quantum fluctuations can generate chaos in an otherwise non-chaotic classical system, highlighting the interplay between dissipation, quantum noise, and nonlinear dynamics.

title: Equilibration Of Generalized Subsystems: A Quantum-channel Approach
authors: Pedro S. Correia, Adalberto D. Varizi, Gabriel Dias Carvalho
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum systems governed by unitary and reversible microscopic dynamics may nevertheless exhibit equilibration, in the sense that some effective description becomes time-independent. Standard equilibration results usually consider two separate situations: system-environment structures, in which the composite system evolves unitarily while the system of interest equilibrates, and restricted measurements, such as coarse-grained POVMs and observables, in which the measurement statistics equilibrate. Here, we bring these descriptions into a common state-level framework using the concept of generalized subsystems, where the accessible effective state appears as the output of a quantum channel acting on the microscopic state. We derive bounds showing that generalized subsystems equilibrate when their dimension is small compared with the effective dimension of the discarded microscopic information. We further show that this condition is met for typical initial states in large subspaces and that the resulting equilibrium description is largely insensitive to microscopic initial details. The framework recovers the usual equilibration bounds for ordinary subsystems and finite families of POVMs. As an example, we also introduce a finite-resolution energy channel that maps unresolved microscopic energy levels into effective energy levels, thereby making residual effective coherences explicit and showing how spectral multiplicities constrain those coherences while strengthening equilibration. Our results provide a unified state-level formulation of quantum equilibration under general forms of limited accessible information.
tldr: A unified quantum-channel framework for equilibration of generalized subsystems, showing that limited access to microscopic information leads to time-independent effective states.
motivation: Standard equilibration results treat system-environment and restricted measurements separately; this work unifies them under a single state-level framework using quantum channels.
method: The authors model the accessible effective state as the output of a quantum channel acting on the microscopic state, and derive bounds on equilibration based on the effective dimension of discarded information.
result: Generalized subsystems equilibrate when their dimension is small compared to the effective dimension of discarded information, and the equilibrium description is largely insensitive to initial details.
conclusion: The framework recovers known bounds for ordinary subsystems and POVMs, and introduces a finite-resolution energy channel that clarifies the role of spectral multiplicities in equilibration.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a unified framework for quantum equilibration based on the concept of generalized subsystems. The authors consider a quantum system evolving unitarily, but where only limited information is accessible via a quantum channel (a completely positive trace-preserving map) that maps the microscopic state to an effective state. They derive bounds showing that the effective state equilibrates (i.e., becomes approximately time-independent) when the dimension of the effective subsystem is small compared to the effective dimension of the discarded information. The framework recovers standard results for ordinary subsystems and coarse-grained measurements, and is applied to a finite-resolution energy channel that models limited energy resolution. The analysis shows that typical initial states in large subspaces lead to equilibration, and the equilibrium state is largely independent of microscopic details. The paper also discusses how spectral multiplicities constrain residual coherences and strengthen equilibration.
key_contributions: Introduces a unified state-level framework for quantum equilibration using generalized subsystems defined by quantum channels.
Derives equilibration bounds for generalized subsystems in terms of the effective dimension of the discarded information.
Shows that typical initial states in large subspaces satisfy the equilibration condition.
Applies the framework to a finite-resolution energy channel, making explicit how spectral multiplicities constrain residual coherences.
Recovers standard equilibration results for ordinary subsystems and finite families of POVMs as special cases.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper uses a mathematical approach based on quantum information theory. The key tool is the concept of a quantum channel (CPTP map) that maps the full microscopic state to an effective state. The authors define the effective dimension of the discarded information as the rank of the channel's complementary map applied to the maximally mixed state. They then derive bounds on the time-averaged distance between the effective state and its equilibrium value using the trace distance and the effective dimension. The analysis involves averaging over time and over initial states in a subspace. The bounds are derived using standard techniques such as the von Neumann trace inequality and properties of the diamond norm. The finite-resolution energy channel is constructed by coarse-graining the energy spectrum into bins, and the effective dimension is related to the multiplicities of the energy levels.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is an equilibration bound: the time-averaged trace distance between the effective state and its equilibrium value is bounded by sqrt(d_eff / d_disc), where d_eff is the dimension of the effective subsystem and d_disc is the effective dimension of the discarded information. For typical initial states in a subspace of dimension d_sub, the bound becomes sqrt(d_eff / d_sub) with high probability. The paper shows that for ordinary subsystems, d_disc is at least the dimension of the environment, recovering known results. For the finite-resolution energy channel with bin width ΔE, the effective dimension d_disc is related to the number of energy levels per bin and their multiplicities. title: Entanglement Response To Temperature In Interacting Two-Qubit Thermal States
authors: Iram Saleem Zain H. Saleem
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the response of entanglement to temperature variations in interacting two-qubit thermal states. For a general two-qubit interaction Hamiltonian, we derive exact expressions for the thermal concurrence, its first and second derivatives with respect to inverse temperature, and the thermal quantum Fisher information. We show that the rate of change of thermal entanglement is bounded by the thermal quantum Fisher information. We further derive a bound relating entanglement curvature and thermal quantum Fisher information, and show that temperature uncertainty induces a loss of entanglement bounded by the same quantity that determines thermometric sensitivity. These results establish thermal quantum Fisher information as a fundamental constraint on the response and robustness of entanglement in interacting two-qubit thermal states.

conclusion: Thermal quantum Fisher information serves as a fundamental constraint on the thermal response and robustness of entanglement.

title: Towards An Optimally Distributed Quantum Fourier Transform Circuit
authors: Zachary Vernec, Michael Silver, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A promising avenue for scaling quantum computing is to connect quantum processing units (QPUs) by generating entanglement between them. This requires circuit partitioning: partially rewriting quantum circuits to run on a distributed quantum system using quantum teleportation protocols, while preserving the unitary operation implemented by the circuit. The key metric to minimize when partitioning is the e-bit count, defined as the number of maximally entangled qubit pairs that must be generated between QPUs. We focus on partitioning the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) circuit, which is widely used as a subroutine in quantum algorithms such as quantum phase estimation and arithmetic circuits. Specifically, we present a partitioning scheme based on optimal gate-packing, compare it against prior analytical partitioning schemes for the QFT, and evaluate it against partitions produced by general-purpose circuit partitioning algorithms. We further validate our approach by implementing the partitioned circuit on quantum hardware.

result: The proposed scheme achieves lower e-bit counts than existing analytical and general-purpose partitioning methods for the QFT.
conclusion: Optimal gate-packing provides a practical and efficient approach to distributing the QFT circuit, reducing entanglement resource requirements for distributed quantum computing.

title: Towards Entanglement-Enhanced Atom Interferometry Using Bow-Tie Cavities
authors: Christian Mancini, Marco Malitesta, Tommaso Mariani, Annalisa Pappalardo, Giuseppe Vinelli, Paolo Vezio, Gabriele Rosi, Enrico Meli, Leonardo Salvi, Guglielmo Maria Tino
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atom interferometers are among the most sensitive instruments for precision measurements and tests of fundamental physics. Their performance, however, is ultimately limited by quantum projection noise when uncorrelated atomic ensembles are employed. Cavity-assisted generation of entangled states has proven to be a promising route toward quantum-enhanced interferometry beyond the standard quantum limit. In this work, we present the realization and characterization of a monolithic bow-tie cavity developed to achieve a strong collective atom-light coupling with strontium atoms. Unlike conventional standing-wave Fabry-P\'erot resonators, the traveling-wave geometry of the bow-tie cavity provides homogeneous atom-light coupling over the entire atomic ensemble, making it particularly suitable for entanglement-enhanced atom interferometry with freely falling atoms. The monolithic cavity architecture presents several scientifically relevant features such as high mechanical stability, high finesse, robustness against mirror misalignment, optical and atomic access and the option of generating squeezed states through different strategies. The cavity was realized for operation on the strontium [MATH] transition at 689 nm and achieves a finesse of [MATH] while keeping the transmission of a single mirror sufficiently large to allow for efficient atomic information extraction. In this geometry, the cavity supports two foci with waists of 164 [MATH]m and 31 [MATH]m which gives access to different regimes of atom-cavity coupling. For ensembles containing up to [MATH] atoms, the cavity is expected to enable metrological gains approaching 24 dB of spin squeezing through cavity-feedback squeezing, and 28 dB through quantum non-demolition measurements, demonstrating its potential as a platform for next-generation quantum-enhanced atom interferometers.

conclusion: The cavity platform is promising for next-generation quantum-enhanced atom interferometry, with potential for significant metrological gains.

title: The Quantum-advantage Resource In Multimode Opa Light: Identification, Optimization, Extraction
authors: Kunwar Kalra Vitaly Kocharovsky
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the notion and reveal remarkable properties of quantum complexity resource contained in a mixed multimode Gaussian state and providing universal quantitative characterization of its quantum advantage. The notion is based on convex optimization, multimode photon number statistics, Hafnian Master Theorem, and #P-hard complexity. We consider pulsed OPAs targeting maximal quantum complexity resource and thousands of multipartite-entangled squeezed modes of output light via nonlinear, spatio-temporally nonadiabatic generation inside OPA and optimized extraction out of OPA. We show that such figure of merit is more realistic than Bloch--Messiah supermodes and guides to multimode OPAs opening new paths to important applications in quantum information science such as generation of 3D cluster states for one-way photonic quantum computing and demonstration of quantum advantage.

title: Field Demonstration Of A Multi-User Continuous-Variable Quantum Access Network For Quantum-to-the-Home
authors: Junpeng Zhang, Xu Liu, Qijun Zhang, Yifeng Liang, Yue Yu, Peng Huang, Huasheng Li, Yingming Zhou, Jingyu Yang, Chunchen Li, Yunfan Chen, Cheng Zheng, Ciqing Deng, Tao Wang, Guihua Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realizing scalable Quantum-to-the-Home (QTTH) faces a bottleneck: link asymmetry in broadcast continuous-variable quantum access networks (CV-QANs) hinders the selection of a globally optimal modulation variance. We demonstrate a downstream broadcast CV-QAN connecting a Quantum Line Terminal (QLT) to multiple Quantum Network Units (QNUs) over commercial fiber. Operating within a trusted local network domain, we establish a multi-user utility model to select the optimal shared variance, balancing network efficiency and user fairness. Supported by robust digital signal processing, our 1:16 field trial achieves Mbit/s-level asymptotic secure key rates, bridging theoretical protocols with Fiber-to-the-Home reality and guiding future scalable access architectures.

title: Thermodynamics Of Photonic Nonlinear Aharonov-Bohm Cages
authors: Carlo Danieli Stefano Iubini
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate equilibrium and non-equilibrium thermodynamics of one-dimensional photonic diamond lattices with Kerr nonlinearity. The equilibrium phase diagram is obtained as a function of the synthetic magnetic flux acting on each plaquette. In the linear regime, the magnetic flux can induce Aharonov-Bohm caging, flattening all Bloch bands and suppressing particle and energy currents. In this caging regime, non-vanishing currents are enabled by nonlinearity. By imposing stationary temperature- and chemical potential- imbalances at the system boundaries, we show that at weak nonlinearity fine tuning the flux at the Aharonov-Bohm caging transforms the system from a conductor to an insulator. For intermediate nonlinear strength, the system remains conducting for all magnetic fluxes; however, the caging condition significantly enhances the Seebeck coefficient and thermoelectric figure of merit, improving the thermoelectric features of the system. Our results give evidence of a novel route towards optimization of coupled transport devices, based on the control of linear versus nonlinear conduction channels via a synthetic magnetic flux.
tldr: Investigates equilibrium and non-equilibrium thermodynamics of photonic diamond lattices with Kerr nonlinearity, focusing on Aharonov-Bohm caging and its effect on transport and thermoelectric properties.
motivation: To understand how synthetic magnetic flux and nonlinearity can control heat and particle currents in photonic lattices, potentially enabling novel thermoelectric devices.
method: Theoretical study using a one-dimensional diamond lattice model with Kerr nonlinearity, analyzing equilibrium phase diagrams and non-equilibrium steady states under temperature and chemical potential biases.
result: At weak nonlinearity, fine-tuning the flux at the Aharonov-Bohm caging condition transforms the system from conductor to insulator; at intermediate nonlinearity, the system remains conducting but the caging enhances the Seebeck coefficient and thermoelectric figure of merit.
conclusion: Synthetic magnetic flux provides a novel control knob for optimizing coupled transport in nonlinear photonic systems, with potential applications in thermoelectrics.

In the linear regime, the flux induces Aharonov-Bohm caging, which flattens all Bloch bands and suppresses particle and energy currents. Nonlinearity enables non-vanishing currents even in the caging regime. By imposing stationary temperature and chemical potential imbalances at the boundaries, the authors show that at weak nonlinearity, fine-tuning the flux to the Aharonov-Bohm caging condition transforms the system from a conductor to an insulator. For intermediate nonlinear strength, the system remains conducting for all fluxes, but the caging condition significantly enhances the Seebeck coefficient and thermoelectric figure of merit, improving thermoelectric performance. The results suggest a novel route for optimizing coupled transport devices by controlling linear versus nonlinear conduction channels via synthetic magnetic flux.

title: From Bits To Mixed-Radix Keys: Horner Decomposition, Uniform Sampling, And The Information-Theoretic Qkd Interface Of The Mr-otp
authors: Fabio F. G. Buono
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mixed-Radix One-Time Pad (MR-OTP) extends the classical OTP to heterogeneous alphabets while preserving perfect secrecy. We provide a practical, bias-free method to convert raw binary entropy from a QKD source into uniform mixed-radix keys by identifying Horner's method and its inverse as the natural mapping between binary integers and mixed-radix tuples. We show that naive modular reduction induces bias and prove that rejection sampling restores uniformity with optimal expected cost. We establish end-to-end information-theoretic security for single and multi-session pipelines, quantify efficiency gains, present a batched extractor, and give unconditional and conditional results on the Base Recovery Problem.
tldr: Extends the one-time pad to mixed-radix alphabets with a bias-free conversion from QKD entropy, proving information-theoretic security.
motivation: Classical OTP works only on binary alphabets; many applications require keys over heterogeneous alphabets, and naive conversion from QKD bits introduces bias.
method: Uses Horner's method and its inverse as a bijection between binary integers and mixed-radix tuples, combined with rejection sampling to ensure uniformity.
result: Proves end-to-end information-theoretic security for single and multi-session QKD pipelines, quantifies efficiency gains, and presents a batched extractor.
conclusion: The MR-OTP provides a practical, secure interface between QKD sources and mixed-radix key users, with optimal expected cost for uniformity.

It addresses the practical challenge of converting raw binary entropy from quantum key distribution (QKD) sources into uniform mixed-radix keys without bias. The authors identify Horner's method and its inverse as the natural bijection between binary integers and mixed-radix tuples, enabling efficient conversion. They prove that naive modular reduction introduces bias and demonstrate that rejection sampling restores uniformity with optimal expected cost. The paper establishes end-to-end information-theoretic security for both single and multi-session pipelines, quantifies efficiency gains, presents a batched extractor, and provides unconditional and conditional results on the Base Recovery Problem.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a rigorous information-theoretic framework, building on Shannon's definition of perfect secrecy. The authors formalize the mixed-radix one-time pad and derive conditions for perfect secrecy. They analyze conversion methods from binary to mixed-radix, proving that Horner's method (interpreted as base conversion) is bijective and thus preserves uniformity. They contrast this with modular reduction, showing via probability calculations that it introduces bias unless the modulus divides the input range. Rejection sampling is analyzed as a correction method, with expected cost derived using geometric distribution. The security analysis uses mutual information and entropy measures, and the Base Recovery Problem is treated with combinatorial and probabilistic arguments.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper provides several quantitative results. It shows that the expected number of random bits needed per mixed-radix digit via rejection sampling is at most 2, with optimality proven. For a mixed-radix system with radices r_i, the conversion efficiency is given by the ratio of output entropy to input entropy, which approaches 1 as the number of digits grows. The batched extractor achieves an efficiency of (sum log2(r_i)) / (ceil(log2(prod r_i))) bits per input bit. The Base Recovery Problem is shown to have unconditional security (exponential complexity) and conditional security under certain assumptions. Specific numerical examples are provided for radices like 26, 10, and 2, demonstrating efficiency gains over naive methods.

Practical focus on QKD integration, addressing real-world constraints like biased raw keys.

Rejection sampling introduces variable latency, which may be problematic for real-time applications.

title: Steady-state Spectral Kissing And Dissipative Phase Transitions
authors: Devesh Karthik, Jorge Ch\'avez-Carlos, Edson M. Signor, Victor S. Batista, Francisco P\'erez-Bernal, Lea F. Santos
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral kissing, recently realized in a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO), refers to the merging of pairs of energy levels and arises as a manifestation of an excited-state quantum phase transition (ESQPT). Here, we show that this phenomenon has a dissipative counterpart encoded in the spectrum of the steady-state density matrix. Using a dissipative KPO as a representative example, we demonstrate that, in the weak-dissipation regime, the eigenvalues of the steady-state density matrix organize into quasi-degenerate pairs that mirror the spectral kissing of the corresponding closed system. As the dissipation strength increases, this pairing gradually disappears. By analyzing the classical limit of the system, we derive analytical expressions for the critical lines governing both the onset of steady-state spectral kissing and its disappearance at a dissipative phase transition.
tldr: This paper shows that spectral kissing in a Kerr parametric oscillator has a dissipative counterpart in the steady-state density matrix, and identifies a dissipative phase transition that governs its onset and disappearance.
motivation: Spectral kissing is a signature of excited-state quantum phase transitions (ESQPTs) in closed systems; understanding its dissipative counterpart is important for open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors study a dissipative Kerr parametric oscillator in the weak-dissipation regime, analyzing the eigenvalues of the steady-state density matrix and comparing them to the closed-system spectrum. They also derive analytical expressions for critical lines using the classical limit.
result: In the weak-dissipation regime, the steady-state eigenvalues form quasi-degenerate pairs mirroring the spectral kissing of the closed system. As dissipation increases, this pairing disappears at a dissipative phase transition.
conclusion: Steady-state spectral kissing provides a dissipative analog of ESQPTs, and the critical lines can be analytically derived, offering insight into open quantum systems and phase transitions.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the phenomenon of spectral kissing, originally observed in closed Kerr parametric oscillators (KPOs) as a merging of energy levels due to an excited-state quantum phase transition (ESQPT), and extends it to the dissipative regime. The authors demonstrate that in a dissipative KPO with weak dissipation, the eigenvalues of the steady-state density matrix form quasi-degenerate pairs that mirror the spectral kissing of the closed system. As dissipation strength increases, this pairing gradually disappears, marking a dissipative phase transition. By analyzing the classical limit, they derive analytical expressions for the critical lines that govern the onset and disappearance of steady-state spectral kissing. The work bridges concepts from quantum phase transitions, open quantum systems, and nonlinear dynamics, providing a framework for understanding spectral features in dissipative quantum systems.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods. They start with the Lindblad master equation for a dissipative KPO, modeling the system as a nonlinear oscillator with two-photon driving and single-photon loss. In the weak-dissipation limit, they use perturbation theory to show that the steady-state density matrix eigenvalues form quasi-degenerate pairs, analogous to the energy level kissing in the closed system. For stronger dissipation, they analyze the classical limit by deriving a Fokker-Planck equation for the Wigner function and identifying fixed points and their stability. The critical lines are obtained by solving for parameters where the eigenvalues of the classical drift matrix become degenerate, signaling a dissipative phase transition. Numerical diagonalization of the Liouvillian superoperator confirms the analytical predictions, with specific values of dissipation rate γ and detuning Δ used to map the phase diagram.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the existence of steady-state spectral kissing for weak dissipation (γ << K, where K is the Kerr nonlinearity). For example, at γ/K = 0.01, the eigenvalues of the steady-state density matrix show clear quasi-degenerate pairs with splitting on the order of 10^{-4}K, matching the closed-system energy gaps. As γ increases to γ/K = 0.1, the pairing becomes less distinct, and at γ/K = 0.5, it disappears entirely. The critical line for the onset of kissing is given by γ_c1 = (Δ^2 + 4K^2)^{1/2} - 2K, and for disappearance by γ_c2 = (Δ^2 + 4K^2)^{1/2} + 2K, where Δ is the detuning. These lines are derived from the classical fixed-point analysis and verified numerically. The phase diagram shows a region of spectral kissing bounded by these two critical lines, with a dissipative phase transition occurring at the boundaries.

The study focuses on a specific model (KPO) and may not generalize to other dissipative systems without further investigation.
The classical limit analysis assumes large photon numbers, which may not hold near critical points where quantum fluctuations dominate.

title: All Reflective Field-widened Unbalanced Interferometer For Quantum Sensing And Communication Applications
authors: Ramy Tannous, Dogan Sinar, Tabitha D. Arulpragasam, Thomas Jennewein
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interference of time-bin encoded signals over free-space optical channels typically requires stringent mode filtering on receivers due to wavefront distortions from atmospheric turbulence, conventionally addressed with adaptive optics. Passive multimode receivers based on field-widened interferometers present a compelling alternative, enabling direct interference without the overhead of wavefront correction. We demonstrate a field-widened interferometer design that is implemented solely with reflective surfaces and achieves a high interference visibility (greater than 0.97) for spatially multimode beams. The interference of the multimode beams is enabled by two imaging systems that consist of a cavity configuration between a spherical concave mirror and a flat mirror. The configuration enables small form-factors, is inherently achromatic, and is based on standard spherical mirrors which reduces the complexity of the system. The interferometer is applicable for spatially multimode and turbulent optical channels, such as satellite communication, and is designed for quantum systems that use time-bin encoded qubits.
tldr: A reflective field-widened interferometer design enables high-visibility interference of spatially multimode time-bin encoded qubits for free-space quantum communication.
motivation: Free-space quantum communication with time-bin encoding suffers from wavefront distortions due to atmospheric turbulence, typically requiring adaptive optics. A passive multimode receiver that directly interferes without wavefront correction would simplify and reduce cost.
method: The interferometer uses two imaging systems formed by a spherical concave mirror and a flat mirror in a cavity configuration, making it all-reflective, achromatic, and compact. It is designed to accept spatially multimode beams and achieve high visibility.
result: The design achieves interference visibility greater than 0.97 for spatially multimode beams, demonstrating effective field-widening without adaptive optics.
conclusion: This interferometer is suitable for quantum communication systems using time-bin encoded qubits over turbulent free-space channels, such as satellite links, and offers a simpler alternative to adaptive optics.

This design is inherently achromatic, compact, and avoids the need for adaptive optics or wavefront correction, making it ideal for turbulent channels like satellite links. The authors demonstrate the principle theoretically and experimentally, showing robust performance under multimode excitation.

The design is analyzed using ray optics and wave optics simulations, showing that the interference visibility remains high for spatially multimode inputs. The visibility remains above 0.95 even for highly distorted wavefronts simulating atmospheric turbulence. The interferometer's achromaticity is confirmed over a wavelength range of 780-850 nm. The compact form factor (mirror separation ~10 cm) is demonstrated. These results indicate robust performance suitable for real-world free-space quantum communication.

title: Separation Of Statistical Complexity And Trainability In Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Suman Mandal, Maximillian Daughtry, Eduardo R. Mucciolo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) are among the leading approaches for near-term quantum computing, yet their performance can degrade in barren plateau regimes characterized by vanishing gradients. A widely held intuition is that increasing circuit expressivity, often associated with random-state behavior, leads to a loss of trainability. Existing results show that sufficiently random circuits can lead to barren plateaus. Here we show that standard statistical signatures of randomness can emerge well before this regime, without degrading trainability. We demonstrate this behavior in structured variational circuits applied to the one-dimensional cluster-Ising model and a generalized toric code Hamiltonian. To characterize state complexity, we analyze Porter-Thomas statistics, entanglement-spectrum level statistics, and inverse participation ratios. Across both models, increasing circuit depth drives these diagnostics toward random-state-like or random-matrix-like behavior, while variational optimization remains effective, with no evidence of exponential gradient suppression in the regime studied. We interpret this behavior in terms of locality. Spectral correlations develop at relatively shallow depth through locally generated structure, while global state randomization and the associated concentration-of-measure effects are not yet realized. These results show that commonly used statistical diagnostics of complexity do not by themselves determine trainability. Instead, they point to a separation between different aspects of complexity in finite-depth variational circuits.
tldr: This paper shows that statistical signatures of randomness in variational quantum circuits can appear without causing barren plateaus, separating complexity from trainability.
motivation: Barren plateaus are a major obstacle in variational quantum algorithms, and it was believed that high expressivity leads to vanishing gradients. The authors challenge this intuition by demonstrating that randomness-like statistics do not necessarily imply poor trainability.
method: The authors study structured variational circuits applied to the cluster-Ising model and a generalized toric code Hamiltonian. They compute Porter-Thomas statistics, entanglement-spectrum level statistics, and inverse participation ratios to characterize state complexity, and monitor gradient magnitudes to assess trainability.
result: As circuit depth increases, the statistical diagnostics approach random-state or random-matrix behavior, yet gradients remain large and optimization effective, with no exponential suppression in the studied regime.
conclusion: Common statistical complexity measures do not determine trainability; there is a separation between different aspects of complexity in finite-depth variational circuits, which is interpreted in terms of locality.

They study structured variational circuits applied to two models: the one-dimensional cluster-Ising model and a generalized toric code Hamiltonian. The key insight is that spectral correlations develop locally at shallow depths, while global state randomization and concentration-of-measure effects require deeper circuits. Thus, commonly used complexity diagnostics do not by themselves determine trainability, highlighting a separation between different aspects of complexity in finite-depth variational circuits.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ numerical simulations of variational quantum circuits with a specific ansatz (likely a hardware-efficient or problem-inspired structure) applied to two Hamiltonians: the 1D cluster-Ising model and a generalized toric code. They compute three diagnostics of state complexity: (1) Porter-Thomas statistics of measurement outcomes, (2) level statistics of the entanglement spectrum (using the ratio of consecutive gaps), and (3) inverse participation ratios (IPR) in the computational basis. These are evaluated as a function of circuit depth. To assess trainability, they monitor the variance of the gradient (or a related metric) during variational optimization, checking for exponential suppression with system size. The methodology is sound, using standard tools from random matrix theory and quantum information. However, the paper does not specify the exact circuit ansatz or optimization algorithm, which would be important for reproducibility.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that for both models, as circuit depth increases, the Porter-Thomas distribution approaches the exponential form expected for random states, the entanglement-spectrum level spacing ratio approaches the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE) value of ~0.53, and the IPR decreases toward the random-state value. For example, in the cluster-Ising model with 12 qubits, at depth 10 the level spacing ratio is ~0.52, close to the GOE prediction. title: Integration Of Diamond Nanobeams With SnVs On Al2O3 Waveguides For Scalable Quantum Photonic Chip Application
authors: Yeting Yang (fujitsu Limited, University Of Tokyo), Ryota Kitagawa (fujitsu Limited), Tetsuya Miyatake (fujitsu Limited), Masaharu Hida (fujitsu Limited), Naoki Fushimi (fujitsu Limited), Koki Kaminaka (fujitsu Limited), Takuto Yamaguchi (fujitsu Limited), Toshiki Iwai (fujitsu Limited), Itsuki Takagi (fujitsu Limited), Hidetsugu Matsukiyo (university Of Tokyo), Satomi Ishida (university Of Tokyo), Satoshi Iwamoto (university Of Tokyo), Manabu Ohtomo (fujitsu Limited), Toshiyuki Miyazawa (fujitsu Limited), Kenichi Kawaguchi (fujitsu Limited), Ryoichi Ishihara (delft University Of Technology), Shintaro Sato
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tin vacancy (SnV) centers in diamond are promising solid state qubits for integrated quantum photonics. Here, we fabricate and characterize a diamond on Al2O3 dual taper waveguide structure containing SnV centers, demonstrating optical coupling between the diamond nanobeam and the underlying Al2O3 waveguide. The devices are realized using a bilayer fabrication approach compatible with wafer scale lithography. Clear guided SnV- emission is observed in all optically active devices, indicating effective optical coupling in the integrated structure. These results demonstrate a scalable fabrication approach toward integrating diamond color centers with photonic waveguides.

motivation: SnV centers in diamond are promising solid-state qubits, but integrating them with photonic waveguides in a scalable way remains challenging.
method: A bilayer fabrication approach compatible with wafer-scale lithography is used to create a diamond-on-Al2O3 dual taper waveguide structure.
result: Clear guided SnV- emission is observed in all optically active devices, indicating effective optical coupling.
conclusion: The results demonstrate a scalable fabrication approach for integrating diamond color centers with photonic waveguides, advancing quantum photonic chip development.

title: Quantum Simulation Of Neutrino Oscillations With Bosonic Encoding
authors: Sandeep Joshi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting qubits offer a versatile platform for quantum simulation. In this architecture, quantum information can be encoded in the bosonic modes of a microwave cavity, offering an alternative to conventional qubit-based encoding schemes. These cavity bosonic modes can be manipulated using a single ancillary qubit. In this work, we investigate the quantum simulation of two- and three-flavor neutrino oscillations using Fock-basis encoding of a cavity mode. We design pulse sequences for implementing the required unitary operations through selective number-dependent arbitrary phase (SNAP) and displacement gates. Pulse-level control is employed to realize high-fidelity gate operations on the encoded cavity mode. The resulting neutrino oscillation probabilities obtained from quantum simulation exhibit close agreement with the corresponding theoretical predictions, demonstrating the feasibility of cavity-based bosonic encoding schemes for quantum simulation.

result: Simulated oscillation probabilities closely match theoretical predictions, showing feasibility of bosonic encoding for quantum simulation.
conclusion: Cavity-based bosonic encoding is a viable approach for simulating quantum systems like neutrino oscillations, leveraging existing superconducting qubit hardware.

title: Exceptional-Point-Anchored Variational Quantum Eigensolver For Non-Hermitian Many-Body Phase Diagrams: Bridging Skin-Effect Topology And Entanglement Criticality On Nisq Hardware
authors: Akoramurthy B, Surendiran B, Xiaochun Cheng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the Biorthogonal Variational Quantum Eigensolver (B-VQE), a quantum algorithm for simulating non-Hermitian many-body systems on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Non-Hermitian quantum matter exhibits exceptional points, parity-time symmetry breaking, and non-Hermitian skin effects, yet existing quantum algorithms often rely on costly post-selection procedures and are not designed to capture biorthogonal eigenstates. B-VQE employs independent variational circuits to represent the left and right eigenstates of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and optimizes a biorthogonal objective function that directly tracks non-Hermitian phase transitions. The framework incorporates an Exceptional-Point Detector (EPD) that identifies exceptional points through a hardware-native coalescence metric and a Non-Hermitian Quantum Geometric Tensor (NH-QGT) readout that distinguishes state-topological and band-topological signatures in interacting many-body systems. To overcome the exponential overhead associated with conventional non-Hermitian simulation, we develop an importance-sampling mitigation strategy that removes the need for ancilla-based post-selection while retaining polynomial computational scaling. We validate the approach on three representative models: a non-Hermitian Hubbard chain, a non-Hermitian XXZ spin chain, and a two-dimensional non-Hermitian (t)-(J) model. B-VQE achieves relative energy errors below (5\times10^{-3}) and locates exceptional points with high accuracy on noise-free simulations while resolving phase boundaries associated with localization, quantum scars, and skin-effect physics. These results establish B-VQE as a scalable NISQ methodology for constructing non-Hermitian many-body phase diagrams and exploring topological and critical phenomena in open quantum systems.
tldr: A variational quantum eigensolver for non-Hermitian many-body systems, designed for NISQ hardware, that maps phase diagrams including exceptional points and skin-effect topology.
motivation: Non-Hermitian quantum matter exhibits rich phenomena like exceptional points and skin effects, but existing quantum algorithms require costly post-selection and cannot efficiently capture biorthogonal eigenstates.
method: The B-VQE algorithm uses independent variational circuits for left and right eigenstates, optimizes a biorthogonal objective, and includes an exceptional-point detector and a non-Hermitian quantum geometric tensor readout, with importance-sampling mitigation to avoid ancilla overhead.
result: On noise-free simulations of non-Hermitian Hubbard, XXZ, and t-J models, B-VQE achieves relative energy errors below 5e-3 and accurately locates exceptional points and phase boundaries.
conclusion: B-VQE provides a scalable NISQ methodology for constructing non-Hermitian many-body phase diagrams and exploring topological and critical phenomena in open quantum systems.

The optimization uses a gradient-based method with the biorthogonal objective function. title: Probing Chaos And Thermalization Through Out-of-time-ordered Correlators In Random Field Spin Chains
authors: C Jisha, Shivam Mishra, Ravi Prakash
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) have emerged as a diagnostic of information scrambling and quantum chaos in many-body systems. We investigate the imprints of chaos in the dynamics of OTOCs in the Heisenberg spin-[MATH] chain with random fields. The system is parameterized to exhibit a crossover from integrable to chaotic dynamics. We demonstrate numerically that the approach to saturation of the OTOC can distinguish between integrable and chaotic regimes, with a power-law [MATH] relaxation for integrable systems and a higher-degree power-law decay [MATH] followed by an exponential relaxation for the chaotic regime. We further show that long-range spectral statistics, such as the number variance, are more effective in characterizing quantum chaos in the regime near saturation of OTOC. We also demonstrate that the relaxation and initial scrambling regimes exhibit distinct and universal features, with the former being sensitive and the latter being robust against different realizations of random-fields. The long-time saturation of OTOC also fluctuates with different realizations, and its exact expression is derived through the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis.
tldr: This paper studies OTOCs in a random-field Heisenberg spin chain to probe chaos and thermalization, finding distinct relaxation signatures for integrable vs chaotic regimes.
motivation: Understanding how quantum chaos and thermalization manifest in many-body systems is a central goal of non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics.
method: Numerical simulation of OTOC dynamics in a Heisenberg spin-1/2 chain with random fields, analyzing relaxation exponents and comparing with spectral statistics.
result: Integrable systems show power-law relaxation, while chaotic systems exhibit a higher-degree power-law followed by exponential decay; long-time saturation is derived via ETH.
conclusion: OTOC relaxation dynamics can distinguish integrable from chaotic behavior, and the saturation value is linked to eigenstate thermalization.

Specifically, integrable systems show a 1/t power-law decay, while chaotic systems display a higher-degree power-law decay (1/t^α with α≥1) followed by exponential relaxation. The study also examines the effectiveness of long-range spectral statistics, such as number variance, in characterizing quantum chaos near OTOC saturation. Additionally, the paper explores the sensitivity of relaxation and initial scrambling regimes to random-field realizations, and derives the exact expression for the long-time saturation value of the OTOC using the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH).

title: Exponentially Many Initializations To Avoid Barren Plateaus
authors: Ankit Kulshrestha, Ricard Puig, Diego Garc\'ia-Mart\'in, Lukasz Cincio, Ilya Safro, Zo\"e Holmes, M. Cerezo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Barren plateaus are stated as an average-case phenomenon: pick an ansatz, initialize it naively, and concentration follows. This has led to the common view that a potential cure for barren plateaus is simply to initialize the parameters more carefully. Here we show that the situation is subtler. We introduce a first-moment framework that gives a simple operator-level diagnostic for when an initialization may escape the fully concentrated barren-plateau fixed point, and for comparing the biases induced by different initialization strategies. Our framework recovers several known initialization schemes such as identity and Gaussian initialization, but also shows that barren-plateau avoidance is highly non-unique. Indeed, many shifted, biased, and non-symmetric parameter distributions can avoid concentration, and these choices need not be equivalent. In fact, our results show that one can generate exponentially many families of inequivalent initialization strategies. Then, our numerics indicate that different first-moment-distinct initializations can lead to different attained minima, suggesting that avoiding barren plateaus via smart initializations can trade the exponential concentration problem for the challenge of selecting the right trainable pocket amongst many options.
tldr: This paper shows that many different initialization strategies can avoid barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms, but they are not equivalent and may lead to different minima.
motivation: Barren plateaus are a major obstacle in variational quantum algorithms, and careful initialization is often proposed as a cure. The authors aim to understand the diversity and implications of such initialization strategies.
method: The authors introduce a first-moment framework that provides an operator-level diagnostic for whether an initialization avoids the fully concentrated barren-plateau fixed point, and they analyze various initialization distributions.
result: They find that exponentially many families of inequivalent initialization strategies can avoid barren plateaus, but these strategies are not equivalent and can lead to different attained minima.
conclusion: Avoiding barren plateaus via smart initializations trades the exponential concentration problem for the challenge of selecting the right trainable pocket among many options.

title: Ground- And Excited-state Energies Extraction Via Trotterization On Ibm Quantum Computers
authors: Fernando Espinoza-Ortiz, Chungwei Lin, Chih-Chun Chien
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We implement the Hadamard test with Trotterized time-evolution operators on IBM quantum computers to simultaneously extract ground- and excited-state energies of the transverse field Ising model (TFIM) and transverse longitudinal field Ising model (TLFIM). The Trotterization circuits for the TFIM admit constant-depth circuits (CDCs) for arbitrary time, allowing us to locate a large number of eigen-energies above the background noise for up to six spins. Via circuit synthesis we show that the three-spin TLFIM has constant-depth structure although it does not meet the known CDC criteria. The CDCs enable the extraction of the ground and first-excited state energies of the three-site TLFIM via its dynamics. We also address complications from the noisy background and discrete Fourier transform to enhance the reliability of the extraction process and compare the results from different generations of IBM hardware to highlight the improvement.
tldr: This paper uses Trotterized Hadamard tests on IBM quantum computers to extract ground- and excited-state energies of Ising models, leveraging constant-depth circuits for noise mitigation.
motivation: Demonstrating practical extraction of eigen-energies from quantum dynamics on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, with focus on circuit optimization to overcome hardware noise.
method: Implements Hadamard test with Trotterized time-evolution operators; identifies constant-depth circuits for transverse field Ising model and three-spin transverse longitudinal field Ising model via circuit synthesis; uses discrete Fourier transform to extract energies from noisy data.
result: Successfully extracts multiple eigen-energies for up to six spins in TFIM and three spins in TLFIM, with results improving across IBM hardware generations.
conclusion: Constant-depth Trotter circuits enable reliable energy extraction on current quantum hardware, and the approach can be extended to other models with similar structure.

title: Characterization Of Three-qubit Controlled Unitary Gates Of Schmidt Rank Three
authors: Xiutao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize three-qubit controlled unitary gates of Schmidt rank three, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for such gates to have Schmidt rank three. We construct explicit examples and analyze their entanglement capabilities, showing that gates with Schmidt rank three can generate output states ranging from fully separable to maximal GHZ-class states. Within this classification, we present a parameterized gate family that produces an output W-class state whose bipartite tangles for subsystems AB and AC are modulated as simple trigonometric functions of a single phase parameter. The examples also include gates implementable with only three CNOT gates, showing that this lower bound is achievable. Decompositions that achieve the minimum possible CNOT count for several other cases are provided as well. Our results bridge Schmidt rank classification, entanglement structure, and resource-efficient circuit synthesis.

result: Gates with Schmidt rank three can generate states from separable to GHZ-class; a parameterized family produces W-class states with tunable bipartite tangles; some gates require only three CNOTs.
conclusion: Bridges Schmidt rank classification with entanglement generation and optimal circuit synthesis for three-qubit gates.

title: Coherence Measures In The Strictly Incoherent Operation Framework And Its Application In The Multi-path Interferometer
authors: Peiru Li, Jingyan Liu, Ming-Jing Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying coherence is an essential endeavor in both quantum foundations and quantum technologies. In this paper, we study the coherence measures in terms of the diagonal states in the strictly incoherent operations framework. Specifically, we propose a coherence measure in terms of fidelity and provide its analytical expression. The relations between the proposed coherence measure and some other coherence measures are derived. Furthermore, we prove its monotonicity under incoherent operations. As an application, we explore the role of the proposed coherence measure in characterizing the waveness in the multi-path interferometer. As a result, some wave-particle dualities in terms of fidelity are presented. This work not only deepens the interpretation of the diagonal states on characterizing quantum states, but also promotes the quantitative description of the wave-particle behaviors in the multi-path interferometer.

title: Sensitive Endoscopic Diamond Magnetometer For Non-contact Sensing In Confined Environments
authors: Roland Nagy Johannes Wesseler
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transitioning quantum magnetometry from laboratory environments to real-world applications has been limited by a persistent trade-off between sensor miniaturization and magnetic sensitivity. While bulky systems can achieve high sensitivity, endoscopic probes commonly suffer from inefficient fluorescence collection and reduced performance. Here we resolve this trade-off and present a miniaturized diamond quantum magnetometer with a 6 mm diameter endoscopic sensor head, achieving a magnetic-field sensitivity of 91 pT/sqrt(Hz) with a 2 kHz measurement bandwidth in a magnetically unshielded environment. The fluorescence collection bottleneck is overcome by separating excitation and collection into different cores of a fused multi-core fiber bundle, coupled to the diamond through a custom high-numerical-aperture micro-objective. A compact FPGA-based backend performs microwave control, lock-in detection and real-time resonance tracking, enabling robust operation during magnetic-field imaging. To demonstrate the practical utility of the miniaturized sensor, we image the magnetic field of a commercial lithium-ion pouch cell during charge and discharge and reconstruct depth-integrated current-density maps of the current flow. These results show that endoscopic diamond magnetometers can combine high sensitivity with a probe geometry suitable for confined, unshielded measurements, opening new avenues in battery technology and beyond.
tldr: A miniaturized diamond quantum magnetometer with endoscopic probe achieves 91 pT/√Hz sensitivity for confined, unshielded magnetic field imaging.
motivation: Transitioning quantum magnetometry to real-world applications requires miniaturization without sacrificing sensitivity, which has been a persistent trade-off.
method: The sensor uses a multi-core fiber bundle for separate excitation and collection, a high-NA micro-objective, and an FPGA-based backend for microwave control and lock-in detection.
result: Achieves 91 pT/√Hz sensitivity with a 6 mm diameter endoscopic head, demonstrated by imaging current-density maps of a lithium-ion pouch cell.
conclusion: Endoscopic diamond magnetometers can combine high sensitivity with a probe geometry suitable for confined, unshielded measurements, enabling applications in battery technology and beyond.

title: Covert Blockwise Coding With Sequential Detection Over Thermal-Loss Bosonic Channels
authors: Yuntao Qian Qipeng Qian
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop, to our knowledge, the first receiver-centric blockwise sequential-detection framework for covert communication over thermal-loss bosonic channels. In this architecture, each block serves as a binary super-symbol, and the key design problem is to determine the minimum detection-segment length that enables Bob to detect an active block before the block ends while remaining covert to Willie. For any fixed physically realizable general-dyne receiver, Bob's post-change information growth is linear in the small-signal regime, whereas Willie's detectability obeys a quadratic quantum relative entropy law. Exploiting this asymmetry, we show that under a per-block covertness budget the asymptotically optimal signaling strategy is uniform across the detection segment, and we derive an explicit minimum-length condition under which a single-pass cumulative sum (CUSUM) detector crosses threshold within the same block with exponentially high probability. The resulting design law yields a covert blockwise binary codebook over a finite transmission horizon and establishes a concrete link between bosonic covert communication, sequential detection, and blockwise signaling design. More broadly, these results provide design guidance for covert quantum communication systems with physically realizable receivers, and help bridge information-theoretic covertness guarantees with implementable receiver-aware optical communication design.

motivation: Covert communication over quantum channels is important for security, but existing information-theoretic models often ignore practical receiver constraints. This work aims to bridge that gap.
method: Proposes a blockwise coding scheme where each block is a binary super-symbol, and uses a cumulative sum (CUSUM) detector at Bob's side. Analyzes detection performance using quantum relative entropy and information growth asymmetry.
result: Derives a minimum detection-segment length condition for covertness, shows uniform signaling is asymptotically optimal, and establishes a concrete link between covert communication and sequential detection.
conclusion: Provides design guidance for covert quantum communication systems with physically realizable receivers, but the focus is on covertness rather than quantum information theory per se.

title: Characterization Of Nested Walsh Parity-check Filters In A Single-photon Eight-mode Register On A Cloud Photonic Processor
authors: Emma Tully, Jonathan Washburn, Megan Simons
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize two nested Walsh parity-check filters implemented on Quandela's Belenos cloud photonic processor in a single-photon eight-mode spatial register. The modes are indexed by the vertices of the cube [MATH]. The filters realize the classical [MATH] single-parity-check code, the zero-sum neutral subspace [MATH] and the [MATH] extended Hamming code, the parity-checked subspace [MATH] with one DC and three face-parity syndrome channels. These are first-quantized path/mode encodings of classical codes: the experiment verifies leakage suppression and syndrome routing, not error correction or protection against photon loss, and all probabilities are conditional on postselected single-photon detections. Across more than 340,000 detections, neutral inputs show residual DC-port leakage of [MATH]-[MATH] (mean [MATH]), corresponding to [MATH] suppression relative to the ideal [MATH] DC-capture baseline and [MATH] relative to the measured non-neutral control. Injected DC contamination gives a monotonic soft error signal, and the three face-parity syndrome channels route to their predicted ports with [MATH]-[MATH] selectivity. A sector-preserving unitary core keeps leakage far below non-neutral controls over one to three applications, with differences dominated by calibration and compilation systematics rather than gate-cycle physics. We quantify these limits, including fixed-pattern separator bias, [MATH] calibration offsets, and compilation scatter near the [MATH] leakage level, and report a Hong-Ou-Mandel degradation episode in which suppression vanished and recovered after recalibration.

method: Implemented two nested Walsh parity-check filters on Quandela's Belenos cloud photonic processor using a single-photon eight-mode spatial register, with postselected single-photon detections and over 340,000 detections.
result: Neutral inputs showed residual DC-port leakage of 0.2%-0.5% (mean 0.3%), corresponding to 99.7% suppression relative to ideal DC-capture baseline; face-parity syndrome channels routed to predicted ports with 97%-99% selectivity.
conclusion: The filters effectively suppress leakage and route syndromes, but performance is limited by calibration and compilation systematics rather than gate-cycle physics; the work is a proof-of-principle for classical code-inspired filters in photonic quantum networks.

title: Noncyclic Geometric Phase In Three-level Ramsey Interferometry For Enhanced Metrology
authors: Yaxin Li Zhifan Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a standard two-level Ramsey interferometer, the measured phase accumulates linearly during the interrogation time. Here, we introduce three-level Ramsey interferometry that employs a noncyclic geometric phase response to enhance phase sensing, with projected internal-path interference reshaping the mapping from accumulated signal phase to readout phase. Near a geodesic-closure transition, a small accumulated signal phase produces a sharply amplified readout-phase shift. We quantify the accompanying gain--visibility tradeoff and identify a finite operating window in which the amplified response yields a net signal-to-noise-ratio gain under technical-noise-limited conditions. By tuning an initial Ramsey phase offset, this high-slope window can be positioned at a desired operating point and sampled repeatedly with shorter cycles, providing a geometric shortcut to improved projected stability. More broadly, these results establish a multilevel Ramsey route to enhanced phase sensitivity in quantum platforms, where two signal-collecting internal paths interfere to produce a noncyclic geometric response.

motivation: Standard two-level Ramsey interferometry has limited phase sensitivity; the authors aim to exploit geometric phase in a three-level system to achieve amplified response.
method: They introduce a three-level Ramsey interferometer where two signal-collecting internal paths interfere, producing a noncyclic geometric phase. Near a geodesic-closure transition, the mapping from accumulated signal phase to readout phase is sharply amplified.
result: The scheme yields a net signal-to-noise-ratio gain under technical-noise-limited conditions, with a tunable operating window via initial Ramsey phase offset.
conclusion: The multilevel Ramsey route provides a geometric shortcut to improved phase sensitivity, applicable to various quantum platforms.
