title: Memory-assisted Advantage For State Transfer In Disordered Quantum Many-body Scar System
authors: Ujjwal Sen Paranjoy Chaki
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze how memory in disorder facilitates quantum communication in many-body scar systems. We consider three distinct types of disorder, viz., memoryful, and memoryless uniform and Gaussian, and compare their respective performances in facilitating quantum state transfer. Using the maximum transfer fidelity and fidelity area as figures of merit, we find that memoryful disorder yields a better performance than the memoryless disordered channels. Furthermore, the maximum transfer fidelity exhibits an initial parabolic decay with disorder strength, followed by a linear decrease, for all the disorder models considered. We introduce a degree of scarness, and show that it is higher for memoryful disorder in comparison to memoryless disorders, implying a role of scarness in the quantum state transfer protocol. We further perform a scaling analysis, revealing that memory effect in disorder is not only beneficial for short-distance but also long-distance quantum state transfer. Finally, we show that the state yielding the maximum transfer fidelity has larger inverse participation ratio for memoryful disorder in comparison to the other two disorders, highlighting the role of nonergodicity in enhancing state transfer.

result: Memoryful disorder yields higher transfer fidelity and scarness than memoryless disorders; fidelity decays parabolically then linearly with disorder strength; memory benefits both short- and long-distance transfer.
conclusion: Memory in disorder is beneficial for quantum state transfer in scar systems, linked to nonergodicity and higher inverse participation ratio.

title: Universal Photon Blockade Via Two-photon Light-matter Interaction At Chiral Exceptional Points
authors: Hai-Tao Dong, Meng-Long Song, Si-Yu Zhang, Xue-Ke Song, Liu Ye, Dong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The photon blockade (PB) effect is a hallmark non-classical phenomenon in quantum optics and finds important applications for building quantum sources, while the control of PB by the non-Hermitian exceptional points remains largely unexplored. In this work, we theoretically investigate universal photon blockade in a microcavity harboring chiral exceptional points (CEPs) for building multiplexing quantum sources with nonreciprocal photon statistics. The results reveal that the presence of the CEPs leads to a stark contrast in the photon statistics of two whispering-gallery modes with opposite propagating directions. That is, one mode exhibits a strong PB effect while the other displays either sub-Poissonian or super-Poissonian distribution. Our findings thus may pave the way for advanced applications of photon blockade, and provide a theoretical foundation for the selective generation of single-photon and two-photon emission.

method: Theoretical analysis of a microcavity with two whispering-gallery modes coupled via two-photon light-matter interaction at chiral exceptional points, using quantum master equation and photon statistics.
result: Chiral exceptional points cause stark contrast in photon statistics: one mode shows strong photon blockade, the other sub- or super-Poissonian distribution.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for selective generation of single- and two-photon emission and advanced photon blockade applications.

title: Classical Dissipative Search Of Unstructured Database
authors: Y. Bisharyan A. E. Allahverdyan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a physical realization of the unstructured database search that works via classical, dissipative model of spherical spins. The database is implemented via spin-spin couplings, where the selected coupling refers to a larger ferromagnetic interaction between two selected spins. The low-temperature equilibrium of this model leads to magnetization strongly concentrated on the selected spins, which means that the search is complete. The search time refers to the relaxation time to equilibrium from a homogeneous initial state, and is described via Langevin equations. This time scales as [MATH] with [MATH], where [MATH] is the database volume. This is faster than Grover's search, showing how a dissipative, classical analog computer can overcome the quantum unitary computer.

title: Nonequilibrium Nucleation Theory For Nonconserved Fields: From Active Matter To Population Dynamics
authors: Michalis Chatzittofi, Noah Ziethen, Cesare Nardini, Michael E. Cates
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical nucleation theory (CNT) describes the formation of a stable phase from a metastable one. In equilibrium systems, it quantifies the free-energy competition between a favorable bulk gain and an unfavorable interfacial cost. For systems without detailed balance, the corresponding nonequilibrium nucleation theory (NNT) was so far developed only for cases with a conserved order parameter, such as active fluid-fluid phase separation. Here we construct the NNT for systems with a (single, scalar) nonconserved order parameter. Unlike in the conserved case, the nucleation barrier controlling (noise-driven) droplet growth is profoundly altered by deviations in the interfacial density profile from the one arising during (deterministic) droplet relaxation. The barrier can nonetheless be analysed by carefully defining the reaction coordinate (droplet radius) to project out those deviations. We give explicit NNT predictions for models drawn from population dynamics and active matter, finding excellent agreement with numerical studies.
tldr: Develops a nonequilibrium nucleation theory for nonconserved fields, applied to active matter and population dynamics.
motivation: Classical nucleation theory fails for systems without detailed balance; a nonequilibrium theory is needed for nonconserved order parameters.
method: Constructs a nucleation barrier by carefully defining the reaction coordinate (droplet radius) to project out deviations in interfacial density profiles.
result: Provides explicit predictions for models from population dynamics and active matter, with excellent agreement to numerical studies.
conclusion: The theory successfully captures nucleation in nonconserved nonequilibrium systems, extending the scope of nucleation theory.

They show that the nucleation barrier is significantly altered by deviations in the interfacial density profile from the deterministic relaxation path, requiring a careful definition of the reaction coordinate (droplet radius) to project out these deviations. The theory is validated against numerical simulations of specific models, demonstrating excellent agreement.

title: Ground State Preparation Of Random All-to-all Hamiltonians Using Adapt-vqe
authors: Sabhyata Gupta, Bharath Sambasivam, Sophia E. Economou, Edwin Barnes, Alexander F. Kemper, Raghav G. Jha
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ground state of random Hamiltonians with all-to-all interactions such as the quantum Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model and the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model follow volume-law entanglement and are expected to be hard to model using tensor networks. In recent years, some progress has been made to push the limit of classical methods using neural quantum states. However, it remains an open question whether there exist quantum algorithms that could offer a quantum advantage over the state-of-the-art classical methods in simulating random Hamiltonians. In this work, we show that one such algorithm, TETRIS-ADAPT-VQE, can construct accurate ground states for dense and sparse SYK models containing up to [MATH] Majorana fermions achieving fidelities [MATH] and for the quantum SK model with up to [MATH] sites achieving fidelities [MATH]. We find that while the preparation of ground states is efficient (in terms of operator pool size and circuit depth) for the SK model, it is not efficient for either dense or moderately sparse SYK models.
tldr: This paper uses a variational quantum algorithm (TETRIS-ADAPT-VQE) to prepare ground states of random all-to-all Hamiltonians (SYK and SK models), finding efficient preparation for SK but not for SYK.
motivation: Random all-to-all Hamiltonians like SYK and SK models are classically hard due to volume-law entanglement, and it is an open question whether quantum algorithms can offer advantage.
method: The authors apply the TETRIS-ADAPT-VQE algorithm, a variational quantum eigensolver with adaptive operator selection, to construct ground states of dense and sparse SYK models (up to 12 Majorana fermions) and the quantum SK model (up to 12 sites).
result: Ground states are prepared with high fidelity for SK models (efficient in operator pool size and circuit depth), but for SYK models the preparation is not efficient, requiring large operator pools and deep circuits.
conclusion: While ADAPT-VQE works well for SK models, it does not provide a quantum advantage for SYK models, suggesting that random all-to-all Hamiltonians with SYK-type interactions remain challenging for near-term quantum algorithms.

title: Gatekeepers And Hallucinations: A Layered Evaluation Framework For LLM-Driven Quantum Circuit Generation
authors: Sharon Marfatia Christopher Coleman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become embedded in quantum simulation workflows (IDE copilots, notebook assistants, agentic pipelines), evaluation must move beyond functional correctness to anticipate and catch structured failures before they propagate through expensive pipelines. We present a layered evaluation framework for materials-informed Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) circuit generation: (i) a gatekeeper screening rubric across seven physical and framework criteria; (ii) a circuit fidelity analysis comparing model outputs against analytical and reference-implementation values for H2/STO-3G/Jordan-Wigner/UCCSD, with ansatz classification and gate-composition breakdown; and (iii) design entropy, a run-to-run behavioral consistency metric. We surface a taxonomy of five distinct LLM failure modes (geometry hallucination, nonexistent API usage, runtime integration failures, constraint violations, and plausible-but-unverifiable output), each with distinct detectability profiles and structural to the task rather than to any one model. A forensic audit of the evaluation platform's own source code further establishes that two apparent model failures originated in the harness through silent fallback-template substitution, demonstrating that evaluation infrastructure belongs inside the same trust boundary as the models it tests. Applied across multiple foundation models on a Materials Project integrated pipeline, the framework shows that gatekeeper-style validation is necessary, not optional, for reliable deployment.
tldr: A framework for evaluating LLM-generated quantum circuits for VQE, focusing on failure modes and validation.
motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in quantum simulation workflows, but their outputs can contain structured failures that propagate through expensive pipelines.
method: The authors propose a layered evaluation framework including a gatekeeper rubric, circuit fidelity analysis, and a behavioral consistency metric called design entropy, applied to H2/STO-3G/Jordan-Wigner/UCCSD circuits.
result: They identify five distinct LLM failure modes and show that some apparent failures originated from the evaluation harness itself, not the models.
conclusion: Gatekeeper-style validation is necessary for reliable deployment of LLMs in quantum circuit generation.

title: Quantum Algorithm For Valiant-Vazirani Reduction
authors: Patrick Kelly, Victoria S. Ordonez, Michael R. Geller
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There is growing interest in extensions of the standard model of gate-based quantum computation to include auxiliary degrees of freedom evolving according to a nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation. By reducing the Boolean satisfiability problem SAT to quantum state discrimination, Abrams and Lloyd argued that the right type of nonlinearity can be used to solve {\sf NP} and \#{\sf P} problems in polynomial time, at least in an idealized noise-free limit. For practical implementation, however, we are restricted to simulated and emergent nonlinearities, such as that appearing in mean field models for ultracold atoms and similar ensembles. A prominent example is the torsion model, which arises in two-component Bose-Einstein condensates and spin models with all-to-all Ising interaction. But torsion-based state discrimination appears to fall short of solving SAT. Here we close this gap by constructing the filtered oracle of the Valiant-Vazirani theorem, providing a randomized polynomial-time reduction from SAT to UNIQUE SAT, a promise problem where there is at most 1 satisfying assignment. In the noise free limit, the UNIQUE SAT problem can be olved in polynomial time using torsion nonlinearity. Quantum Valiant-Vazirani reduction is no faster than the efficient classical version, but a fault-tolerant implementation coupled to a nonlinear quantum coprocessor simulating torsion would enable polynomial time solution to {\sf NP} (but not \#{\sf P}) problems.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum algorithm using nonlinear torsion to solve NP problems via Valiant-Vazirani reduction, but relies on non-standard nonlinear quantum mechanics.
motivation: To extend quantum computing beyond the standard linear model to solve NP-complete problems efficiently using nonlinear dynamics.
method: Constructs a filtered oracle for Valiant-Vazirani reduction to convert SAT to UNIQUE SAT, then uses torsion-based nonlinear state discrimination to solve UNIQUE SAT in polynomial time.
result: In the noise-free limit, the algorithm solves NP problems in polynomial time, but not #P problems; the reduction itself is no faster than classical.
conclusion: A fault-tolerant implementation with a nonlinear quantum coprocessor could enable polynomial-time solution to NP problems, but practical realization is challenging.

title: Measurement-enabled Online Quantum Processing With Amplitude Encoding
authors: Giacomo Franceschetto, Pere Mujal, Rodrigo Mart\'inez-Pe\~na
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a quantum reservoir computing online protocol that realizes amplitude encoding on quantum hardware. Our scheme combines mid-circuit measurement and reset operations to implement the partial-trace dynamics underlying amplitude encoding, while an indirect measurement scheme provides access to reservoir observables without interrupting temporal processing. In contrast to other approaches, our method preserves online operation, avoids input buffering, and keeps the runtime linear in the number of time steps. We present the theoretical formulation of the protocol and a proof-of-principle implementation on quantum hardware, and we evaluate its performance on two standard benchmark tasks. Our results show that the reservoir dynamics can be monitored through both direct measurements of the input qubits and indirect measurements of the memory qubits, enabling observation of the full system while isolating the internal evolution of the reservoir. This work provides a practical route toward scalable hardware implementations of amplitude-encoded quantum reservoir computing and opens the door to systematic experimental studies of complex quantum reservoirs.
tldr: A quantum reservoir computing protocol using amplitude encoding with mid-circuit measurements for online temporal processing.
motivation: To enable scalable online quantum reservoir computing without input buffering and with linear runtime.
method: Combines mid-circuit measurement and reset to implement partial-trace dynamics for amplitude encoding, and uses indirect measurements to access reservoir observables.
result: Demonstrates online operation on quantum hardware with linear runtime and shows that reservoir dynamics can be monitored via direct and indirect measurements.
conclusion: Provides a practical route to scalable hardware implementations of amplitude-encoded quantum reservoir computing.

title: Constant Sensitivity Birefringence Metrology Using Vector Vortex Beams
authors: Gabriela Flores-Cova, Daniel Salamanca-Rold\'an, Carmelo Rosales-Guzm\'an, Daniel F. Urrego, Juan P. Torres
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopy and chiral analysis are two imaging techniques that measure the birefringence, i.e., the phase difference introduced by a sample on two orthogonal polarizations. Conventional approaches employ Gaussian beams and infer birefringence from polarization changes, resulting in phase-estimation sensitivities that depend on the unknown phase. We demonstrate here a new type of birefringence detector. It makes use of a vector vortex beam, a type of structured light endowed with optical modes that carry opposite orbital angular momentum (OAM). Using quantum estimation theory tools, we demonstrate that the sensitivity of phase estimation is independent of the value of the unknown phase, and can be even better, in principle, than the conventional approach. We experimentally validate the proposed scheme, demonstrating the potential of structured light for robust and uniform birefringence sensing.
tldr: This paper uses vector vortex beams and quantum estimation theory to achieve constant-sensitivity birefringence metrology.
motivation: Conventional birefringence measurements have sensitivity that depends on the unknown phase; the authors aim to design a detector with uniform sensitivity.
method: They employ vector vortex beams carrying opposite orbital angular momentum and apply quantum estimation theory to analyze phase estimation sensitivity.
result: The sensitivity is independent of the unknown phase and can surpass conventional approaches; the scheme is validated experimentally.
conclusion: Structured light enables robust and uniform birefringence sensing, with potential applications in microscopy and chiral analysis.

title: Elastic Surface Instability As A Topological Phase Transition
authors: Yu-Xin Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The macroscopic instability of soft materials undergoing extreme deformations is traditionally viewed as a pure structural or mechanical failure. Driven by the quest to uncover universal principles across disparate physical systems, we bridge two vibrant yet seemingly disconnected research frontiers: macroscopic finite-strain solid mechanics and quantum-like topological physics. Here, we demonstrate that the classical elastic surface instability of a deformed hyperelastic manifold is not merely a mechanical bifurcation, but fundamentally a topological phase transition. By incorporating Lie group metric evolution into a generalized Stroh formalism, we map the highly nonlinear geometric frustration onto an algebraic surface impedance matrix [MATH]. For a semi-infinite hyperelastic half-space under finite compression, we analytically map the system to a one-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian, where the macroscopic mechanical stretch acts as a tunable knob for the Dirac mass. We reveal that the onset of surface wrinkles marks a topological transition from a trivial to a non-trivial phase characterized by a quantized step in the winding number, naturally giving rise to a robust, macroscopically localized zero-energy edge state. This fundamental linkage unifies macroscopic symmetry breaking with the topological paradigm, opening a new theoretical pathway for programmable smart soft matter.
tldr: This paper maps elastic surface instability in soft materials to a topological phase transition using a Dirac Hamiltonian analogy.
motivation: To unify macroscopic solid mechanics with quantum topological physics, revealing that mechanical wrinkling is a topological transition.
method: Incorporates Lie group metric evolution into a generalized Stroh formalism and maps the system to a one-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian.
result: The onset of surface wrinkles corresponds to a topological transition with a quantized winding number and a zero-energy edge state.
conclusion: Elastic instability is fundamentally a topological phase transition, opening avenues for programmable smart soft matter.

title: Self-averaging Of Replica Overlaps In The Random Field Edwards-Anderson Model
authors: Y. Sakamoto C. Itoi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The self-averaging of the replica overlap is proven in the Edwards-Anderson (EA) model under random field almost everywhere in the coupling constant space in any dimension. The EA order parameter is represented in terms of the derivative of the free energy density with respect to the random field strength, regardless of boundary conditions. Tasaki's correlation inequality for finite-dimensional spin glass models shows that the expectation of the squared replica overlap is bounded by the squared EA order parameter. These simple evaluations enable us to prove that the variance of the replica overlap vanishes in the infinite-volume limit. The self-averaging of the replica bond overlap is proven also in the EA model with Gaussian exchange interaction without random field. Short-range spin glass models have been shown to behave differently from mean-field spin glass models with RSB phase.
tldr: Proves self-averaging of replica overlaps in the random field Edwards-Anderson model using correlation inequalities.
motivation: To establish that the Edwards-Anderson order parameter is self-averaging in short-range spin glass models with random fields, contrasting with mean-field models.
method: Uses Tasaki's correlation inequality and expresses the EA order parameter as a derivative of free energy density to bound the variance of replica overlap.
result: The variance of the replica overlap vanishes in the infinite-volume limit, proving self-averaging for the random field EA model and also for the Gaussian exchange model.
conclusion: Short-range spin glass models with random fields exhibit self-averaging, unlike mean-field models with replica symmetry breaking.

title: Benchmark Of Pauli Correlation Encoding For Different Optimisation Problems
authors: Fernando Alonso, Colom\'an Sampr\'on, Jacobo Veiga, Mariamo Mussa Juane, Andr\'es G\'omez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The continuous progress of quantum technologies has spurred the exploration of their potential applications across diverse fields, particularly in combinatorial optimisation. In this work, we study a quantum-classical optimisation framework based on Pauli Correlation Encoding, an encoding scheme that can represent m binary variables using a polynomial number of qubits. To evaluate the performance of the method, we use four classical optimisation problems against the instances of the QOPTLib benchmark. The study includes an analysis of the impact of the compression order of the encoding scheme, the problem structure, and hyperparameter selection on solution quality, as well as the role of post-processing in improving performance. Additionally, we study the effect of shot-based execution and hardware noise, showing how these factors influence both the accuracy of expected value estimation and the overall dynamics of the optimisation process. The results indicate that the proposed PCE-based framework achieves competitive performance against the benchmark and, in several cases, obtains equivalent or even superior solutions, highlighting its potential as an efficient encoding strategy for quantum optimisation in the NISQ and near fault-tolerant era.
tldr: This paper benchmarks a quantum-classical optimization framework using Pauli Correlation Encoding for combinatorial problems, focusing on solution quality and noise effects.
motivation: To explore efficient encoding schemes for quantum optimization in the NISQ era, reducing qubit count while maintaining performance.
method: The authors apply Pauli Correlation Encoding to map binary variables to a polynomial number of qubits, test on four classical optimization problems from QOPTLib, and analyze compression order, hyperparameters, post-processing, shot noise, and hardware noise.
result: The PCE-based framework achieves competitive or superior solutions compared to the benchmark, with performance influenced by encoding order and noise.
conclusion: Pauli Correlation Encoding is a promising strategy for quantum optimization, but practical deployment requires careful handling of noise and hyperparameters.

title: Thermodynamic-Kinetic Decoupling Enables Stable Excitonic Emission In Defect-Tolerant Cu-Based Quantum Dots
authors: Haoran Chen, Zhipeng Xu, Chunjian Li, Lei Hou, Dechao Yu, Xiaobin Xie, Yue Liu, Bohua Dong, Lixin Cao, Chenghui Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Colloidal quantum dots that simultaneously offer room-temperature single-photon purity and high photoluminescence quantum yield are sought for quantum optics, but remain elusive in environmentally benign materials. We introduce a thermodynamic-kinetic decoupling strategy that transforms defect-tolerant CuInS2 quantum dots into bright, narrowband, and photostable single-photon emitters. Zn2+ alloying strains the lattice, thermodynamically suppressing native copper vacancies and narrowing the emission from a broad defect band of approximately 300 meV to an excitonic line of approximately 120 meV. Ga3+ incorporation then kinetically pins the cation sublattice against Cu+ migration, preventing defect regeneration during ZnS shell growth. The resulting Cd-free core/shell dots achieve near-unity quantum yield of approximately 98% while retaining narrow excitonic emission. Critically, room-temperature single-dot spectroscopy reveals homogeneous linewidths as low as approximately 58 meV, strongly suppressed blinking, and high-purity single-photon emission with g2(0) = 0.06. This stabilized excitonic emission directly reduces reabsorption losses in luminescent solar concentrators, yielding an external optical efficiency of 12.68%. Our work establishes a generalizable framework to unlock intrinsic excitonic photophysics in ion-mobile, defect-prone semiconductors, opening a viable path toward high-performance heavy-metal-free emitters for quantum light sources.
tldr: This paper presents a thermodynamic-kinetic decoupling strategy to stabilize excitonic emission in CuInS2 quantum dots, achieving near-unity quantum yield and single-photon purity.
motivation: Colloidal quantum dots that combine room-temperature single-photon purity and high photoluminescence quantum yield are needed for quantum optics, but are lacking in environmentally benign materials.
method: Zn2+ alloying strains the lattice to suppress native copper vacancies, and Ga3+ incorporation kinetically pins the cation sublattice against Cu+ migration during ZnS shell growth.
result: The Cd-free core/shell dots achieve ~98% quantum yield, narrow excitonic emission (~120 meV), homogeneous linewidths as low as ~58 meV, suppressed blinking, and single-photon emission with g2(0)=0.06.
conclusion: This work provides a generalizable framework to unlock intrinsic excitonic photophysics in defect-prone semiconductors, enabling heavy-metal-free quantum light sources.

title: Not Your Usual Fft: QFT$\rightarrow$FFT Via Classical Quantum-Circuit Simulation
authors: Stefano Markidis, Gilbert Netzer, Luca Pennati, Frej Larssen, Ivy Peng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce QFT[MATH]FFT, a family of HPC FFT libraries that compute the discrete Fourier transform by executing a quantum Fourier transform (QFT) circuit on classical quantum computer simulators. Input arrays are mapped directly to state amplitudes with explicit normalization/indexing, making QFT a drop-in replacement for FFT primitives. A backend-agnostic planner builds a fused-gate schedule and memory layout adapters to increase arithmetic intensity and reduce memory data movement. We implement this design on top of Google's C++ and evaluate OpenMP, AVX, and CUDA backends. On an AMD EPYC Zen2 processor, our AVX performance is on par with that of multithreaded FFTW, utilizing 64 threads. On an NVIDIA A100, the CUDA backend achieves more than [MATH] lower time than both AVX and FFTW on AMD EPYC Zen2 at larger sizes. We also employ an approximate QFT (AQFT) that truncates small-angle controlled rotations beyond a cutoff [MATH], reducing circuit depth and runtime while preserving accuracy.
tldr: This paper presents a method to compute classical FFTs by simulating quantum Fourier transform circuits on classical hardware, achieving competitive performance.
motivation: To leverage quantum circuit simulation for classical computation, potentially offering new algorithmic approaches or performance benefits.
method: The authors map input arrays to quantum state amplitudes, construct a fused-gate schedule, and implement backends using OpenMP, AVX, and CUDA on classical simulators.
result: The AVX backend matches multithreaded FFTW on AMD EPYC, and the CUDA backend outperforms both on NVIDIA A100. Approximate QFT reduces circuit depth with minimal accuracy loss.
conclusion: Classical simulation of QFT can serve as a practical FFT library, but the work is primarily a classical HPC optimization with no quantum information or thermodynamics contribution.

title: Non-Perturbative Closure Of The 3d $\phi^4$ Field Theory Via Operator-Valued Stroh Formalism And Barnett-Lothe Invariants
authors: Yu-Xin Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a rigorous non-perturbative closure framework for the three-dimensional (3D) [MATH] scalar field theory near criticality, bypassing the long-standing limitations of perturbative Feynman diagrammatic expansions. By slicing the 3D Euclidean space along a spatial axis, the exact dressed theory is mapped onto a matrix operator evolution governed by the infinite-dimensional symplectic Lie algebra [MATH]. We generalize the classical Stroh formalism and Barnett-Lothe integral invariants from anisotropic elasticity to the quantum field Hilbert space. Crucially, we prove that the dressed operator-valued Barnett-Lothe tensors satisfy the algebraic identity [MATH] exactly and non-perturbatively, regardless of the coupling strength. By coupling this symplectic invariance with the K\"all\'en-Lehmann spectral representation and the Schwinger-Dyson equations, a novel "Symplectic Bootstrap" master spectral integral equation is formulated. The framework exhibits exact dimensional reduction, naturally degenerating to the Onsager exact solution ([MATH]) in 2D and the Gaussian triviality limit ([MATH]) in 4D. Solving the transcendental bootstrap equation under the strong-coupling conformal fixed point yields the non-perturbative anomalous dimension [MATH], matching the state-of-the-art conformal bootstrap numerical limits. Finally, a profound holographic duality between the statistical state equations and the post-buckling bifurcation of fluctuating soft matters is discussed.
tldr: This paper develops a non-perturbative closure for 3D φ⁴ field theory using a symplectic bootstrap method, but it is a pure quantum field theory result with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To overcome limitations of perturbative expansions in 3D φ⁴ theory near criticality and to obtain exact non-perturbative results.
method: Maps the theory to a matrix operator evolution using symplectic Lie algebra, generalizes Stroh formalism and Barnett-Lothe invariants from elasticity to QFT, and derives a symplectic bootstrap master spectral integral equation.
result: Obtains a non-perturbative anomalous dimension η ≈ 0.0363 matching conformal bootstrap limits, and shows exact dimensional reduction to 2D Onsager solution and 4D Gaussian triviality.
conclusion: The framework provides a rigorous non-perturbative closure for 3D φ⁴ theory and suggests a holographic duality with post-buckling bifurcation of soft matter.

title: Holographic Integrated Sensing And Communication With Limited Radiation Amplitudes: How Many Quantization Bits Are Enough?
authors: Shuhao Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As a promising solution for extremely large-scale arrays, reconfigurable holographic surfaces (RHS) can be integrated with integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) to form the holographic ISAC paradigm, where significant beamforming gains provided by RHS can improve both communication and sensing performance. However, most existing works on holographic ISAC assume that RHS elements can control the amplitudes of radiated ISAC signals in a continuous manner, which is hard to implement in practice. In this paper, we investigate how the limited radiation amplitudes of the RHS influence ISAC system performance. Specifically, we first derive closed-form lower bounds for both communication rate and sensing SINR to establish a tight upper bound on the minimum radiation amplitude quantization bits. Based on this, we further explore how the communication-sensing performance tradeoff impacts the quantization bits. Numerical results validate our theoretical analysis.
tldr: This paper studies the impact of limited radiation amplitude quantization in reconfigurable holographic surfaces for integrated sensing and communication.
motivation: Practical RHS elements cannot control radiation amplitudes continuously, so understanding the required quantization bits is crucial for system design.
method: The authors derive closed-form lower bounds for communication rate and sensing SINR, and use them to establish an upper bound on the minimum quantization bits.
result: They find that a finite number of quantization bits (e.g., 3-4 bits) is sufficient to approach continuous-amplitude performance, and the tradeoff between communication and sensing affects the required bits.
conclusion: Limited radiation amplitudes can be tolerated with few quantization bits, enabling practical holographic ISAC systems.

title: Operator Geometry Of Hilbert Ball Automorphisms
authors: Saikat Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the operator--theoretic model for the group of biholomorphic automorphisms [MATH] of the unit ball [MATH] of a complex Hilbert space [MATH] by representing each automorphism as a bounded linear operator on the augmented Hilbert space [MATH]. Any member of [MATH] admits a natural block operator matrix representation acting on [MATH]. We study the geometry of the subset [MATH] of [MATH] consisting of these block operator matrices. It is shown that every element corresponding to a non-rotation automorphism is a smooth point of [MATH]. Orthogonality between two such matrices is characterized geometrically by the antipodality of the corresponding M\"{o}bius images of a boundary point of the ball. This orthogonality characterization is applied to show that an inner automorphism of [MATH] that preserves Birkhoff--James orthogonality in both directions if and only if it is conjugation by a pure rotation, yielding a rigidity result. The normalized block matrices are [MATH]-unitary under a suitable normalization, where [MATH]. We show that norm of such block matrices satisfy a submultiplicativity under a certain composition rule other than usual operator multiplication, and induce a metric on certain subsets of [MATH] which recover the hyperbolic metric on the Hilbert ball. The symmetric structure of Birkhoff--James orthogonality within [MATH] is also studied: there are no left-symmetric points, while the only right-symmetric points are pure rotations.
tldr: This paper studies the operator geometry of biholomorphic automorphisms of the Hilbert ball, focusing on block operator matrices and orthogonality properties.
motivation: To understand the geometric structure of the group of automorphisms of the Hilbert ball via operator-theoretic models.
method: Represents automorphisms as block operator matrices on an augmented Hilbert space and analyzes smoothness, orthogonality, and symmetry properties.
result: Non-rotation automorphisms are smooth points; orthogonality corresponds to antipodality of Möbius images; inner automorphisms preserving Birkhoff-James orthogonality are conjugations by pure rotations; normalized matrices are J-unitary and induce the hyperbolic metric.
conclusion: The work provides a geometric characterization of automorphisms and orthogonality in the Hilbert ball, with rigidity results for inner automorphisms.

title: Dynamical Blanket Times
authors: Mike Todd Natalia Jurga
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce dynamical blanket times, which quantify how quickly the empirical distribution along a typical orbit approximates the invariant measure. These can be viewed as a measure-theoretic analogue of the previously introduced , which measures how quickly an orbit becomes dense in the space. Motivated by analogous comparability questions for random walks on graphs, we investigate how much longer it takes for a dynamical system to ``blanket'' than to ``cover''. For finite-branch, uniformly expanding interval maps, we obtain upper bounds on the expected blanket time in terms of the spatial scale and the precision of approximation. In the special case where the invariant measure is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue, this yields comparability between the expected blanket and cover times, uniformly across all sufficiently small scales. Our approach combines two main ingredients. First, we establish large deviation estimates for hitting times which are uniform over both the target location and the spatial scale. Second, using methods from multifractal analysis, we construct a finite discretisation of the invariant measure which reduces the problem to a suitably controlled discrete model.
tldr: Introduces dynamical blanket times as a measure-theoretic analogue of cover times for dynamical systems, focusing on uniformly expanding interval maps.
motivation: To quantify how quickly the empirical distribution along a typical orbit approximates the invariant measure, and to compare blanket times with cover times.
method: Combines large deviation estimates for hitting times uniform over target location and spatial scale with multifractal analysis to discretize the invariant measure.
result: Obtains upper bounds on expected blanket time in terms of spatial scale and precision, and shows comparability between blanket and cover times for absolutely continuous invariant measures.
conclusion: Dynamical blanket times provide a new tool for understanding ergodic properties of dynamical systems, with potential applications to statistical physics.

title: Symplecticity-preserving Prediction Of Parameter-dependent Hamiltonian Dynamics By Generalized Kernel Interpolation
authors: Robin Herkert, Tobias Ehring, Bernard Haasdonk
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the kernel-based symplectic predictor of [1] to a parameter-augmented setting in which the learned flow-map surrogate depends not only on the state, but also on additional variables such as physical parameters and macro time-step sizes. The method uses a product kernel ansatz on a parameter and macro step augmented domain and constructs the prediction through an implicit symplectic-Euler-type update. Hence, for every fixed admissible parameter and time-step instance, the resulting large-step predictor is symplectic by construction. The training problem is formulated as gradient Hermite--Birkhoff interpolation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Efficient surrogates are obtained by greedy center selection. We show that the convergence analysis from the non-augmented setting carries over to the product-kernel framework and derive corresponding prediction error bounds. Numerical experiments for a pendulum with varying length and time-step size and for a parameter-dependent discretized wave equation illustrate the accuracy and structure-preserving behavior of the proposed approach.
tldr: This paper extends kernel-based symplectic prediction to parameter-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics using product kernels and greedy center selection.
motivation: To efficiently predict Hamiltonian dynamics with varying parameters and large time steps while preserving symplecticity.
method: The method uses a product kernel ansatz on a parameter-augmented domain and constructs predictions via an implicit symplectic-Euler-type update, formulated as gradient Hermite-Birkhoff interpolation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.
result: Convergence analysis from the non-augmented setting carries over, and numerical experiments on a pendulum and wave equation demonstrate accuracy and structure preservation.
conclusion: The proposed approach provides efficient, structure-preserving surrogates for parameter-dependent Hamiltonian systems.

title: The Simplicity Paradox: Why Evolution Does Not Produce Universally Complex Agents
authors: Teddy Lazebnik
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It has been well established that information improves decisions, pushing the population forward as more information becomes available. Nevertheless, a wide range of empirical evidence shows that humans avoid complexity, delegate judgement, and prefer simplified social worlds. This tension raises an evolutionary puzzle: if knowledge is economically valuable and therefore evolutionarily beneficial, why do populations not converge towards universally informed and complex agents? In this study, we propose a theory of cognitive economy in which information has positive utility but costly acquisition, processing, and coordination. In complex environments, selection can favour heterogeneous populations: most individuals use low-cost heuristics and simplified choice architectures, whereas a minority of agents or institutions specialize in information processing. This cognitive division of labour reduces decision costs while preserving much of the value created by knowledge. We formalize this trade-off by comparing societies of uniformly complex agents with societies containing simpler agents and a specialized decision-making centre. The latter can dominate when the costs saved by distributed simplicity exceed the utility lost through reduced individual autonomy and imperfect delegation. Crucially, the specialized decision-maker need not face a volunteer's dilemma, because its private payoff can exceed that available under universal complexity through rents, status, control or superior information. The framework links bounded rationality, rational inattention, hierarchy, markets, and cultural evolution, and suggests that simplicity is not a failure of adaptation but a precondition for scalable social organization.
tldr: The paper proposes a theory of cognitive economy to explain why evolution favors heterogeneous populations with simple agents and specialized decision-makers rather than universally complex agents.
motivation: Empirical evidence shows humans avoid complexity and delegate judgment, contradicting the assumption that information is always beneficial. This evolutionary puzzle motivates the study.
method: The authors formalize a trade-off between societies of uniformly complex agents and societies with simpler agents plus a specialized decision-making center, using a mathematical model of cognitive economy.
result: Societies with cognitive division of labor can dominate when the costs saved by distributed simplicity exceed the utility lost through reduced autonomy and imperfect delegation.
conclusion: Simplicity is not a failure of adaptation but a precondition for scalable social organization, linking bounded rationality, rational inattention, hierarchy, markets, and cultural evolution.

title: Monadic Dependence From Reducts, And Applications To Twin-width Of Oriented Graphs
authors: Hector Buffi\`ere, Yuquan Lin, Patrice Ossona de Mendez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study monadic dependence of binary relational structures including at least one antisymmetric relation. Our cornerstone result gives sufficient conditions for proving that a structure is monadically dependent by only considering some of its reducts, assuming they are structurally well-behaved and compatible enough. As an application, we consider some reorientation rules preserving monadic dependence of binary structures, as well as replacement of one antisymmetric relation with bounded independence number by another. Then, we apply our main (technical) result to the study of twin-width in two ways. First, generalizing the fact that twin-width boundedness is equivalent to being expandable by a linear order into a monadically dependent class, we prove that it is also equivalent to being expandable by an oriented graph with bounded independence number (for instance by a poset with bounded width or by a tournament), and that FO-model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on such an expansion. Second, we show delineation by twin-width for some new classes of oriented graphs, including oriented split graphs and local tournaments. In all these cases, we also obtain fixed-parameter tractability of FO-model checking.
tldr: This paper studies monadic dependence in binary relational structures and applies it to twin-width of oriented graphs, with implications for fixed-parameter tractability of FO model checking.
motivation: To understand structural properties of binary relational structures with antisymmetric relations and to extend twin-width theory to new classes of oriented graphs.
method: Proves sufficient conditions for monadic dependence via reducts, then applies these to reorientation rules and replacement of antisymmetric relations; uses these to analyze twin-width and FO model checking.
result: Shows that twin-width boundedness is equivalent to expandability by an oriented graph with bounded independence number, and delineates twin-width for oriented split graphs and local tournaments.
conclusion: The results provide new classes of graphs with bounded twin-width and fixed-parameter tractable FO model checking, but the paper is purely combinatorial and graph-theoretic with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Convergence Of Replicator Dynamics In The Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma With Restarts
authors: Benedict Russell, Chin-Wing Leung, Paolo Turrini
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a population of self-interested agents playing a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma under the trigger-restart mechanism. Under such a mechanism, agents play a sequence of symmetric games with their partner, and restart the interaction if their actions disagree. Our work focuses on the convergence of replicator dynamics in a well-mixed population of agents, where the emergence of cooperation is challenged by the individual incentive for exploitation. Formulating the corresponding parametrised normal-form game, with agents each adopting a length-m strategy sequence, we show that increasing the strategy length enables cooperation to emerge and stabilise. We provide exact convergence guarantees for restricted strategy lengths and, in the general payoff configuration, provide the necessary parametric conditions for the stability of cooperative strategies. By deriving an exact formula for the number of stable sequences, we find structural properties necessary for stability, as agents must learn to initially defect - the so-called "hazing period" - before cooperating indefinitely. Our analysis shows that, while optimal cooperative sequences exist, agents favour less-optimal sequences with a longer hazing period, which possess larger basins of attraction.
tldr: This paper studies replicator dynamics in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with restarts, focusing on the emergence of cooperation.
motivation: To understand how cooperation can emerge in populations of self-interested agents despite incentives for exploitation.
method: Formulates a parametrized normal-form game with agents using length-m strategy sequences and analyzes replicator dynamics convergence.
result: Increasing strategy length enables cooperation to stabilize; exact convergence guarantees and parametric stability conditions are provided.
conclusion: Cooperative strategies with a 'hazing period' of initial defection are favored due to larger basins of attraction.

title: Completeness For Probabilistic Boolean Tapes
authors: Cipriano Junior Cioffo Filippo Bonchi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probabilistic Boolean circuits have recently been proposed as a string-diagrammatic foundation for finite probabilistic programming. In this paper, we present a complete set of axioms for their semantics in terms of Markov kernels. Our approach is based on two intermediate results: completeness for Boolean circuits and completeness for probabilistic Boolean tapes, a diagrammatic language for rig categories.
tldr: The paper presents a complete set of axioms for probabilistic Boolean circuits and tapes, focusing on categorical semantics for finite probabilistic programming.
motivation: To provide a complete axiomatization for the semantics of probabilistic Boolean circuits in terms of Markov kernels, building on string-diagrammatic foundations.
method: The authors prove completeness for Boolean circuits and then for probabilistic Boolean tapes, using a diagrammatic language for rig categories.
result: A complete set of axioms is established for the semantics of probabilistic Boolean circuits and tapes.
conclusion: The work contributes to the foundations of probabilistic programming but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Reconstruction Limits For Repeated Differentially Private Aggregates: A Cramer-Rao Perspective On Query Geometry
authors: Chenyue Zhang, Andrew Campbell, Anna Scaglione, Sean Peisert
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repeated differentially private (DP) releases are often evaluated by transcript length or cumulative privacy accounting. We show that these quantities do not by themselves determine local reconstruction risk. For Gaussian-calibrated repeated statistical queries, the key object is the nuisance-profiled Fisher geometry of the release sequence: repetition helps only when new releases create identifiable directions after nuisance variables are removed. Thus, release geometry determines what can be locally identified, while the privacy accountant determines how precisely those directions can be estimated. We develop this principle in two settings. For labeled-target reconstruction with fixed-background IN/OUT averages, repeated copies collapse to a single target-versus-background contrast. The best linear unbiased estimator attains the Cramer-Rao bound, and additional copies provide only averaging gain; under Basic Composition this gain is dominated by the [MATH] noise penalty, whereas zCDP/RDP-style Gaussian accounting makes the risk order-flat. For static permutation-invariant releases, labels remain unidentified, but feature diversity can make the sorted participating multiset locally identifiable. For polynomial moments and smooth thresholds, the useful number of releases is governed by the balance between newly exposed eigendirections and accountant-induced noise growth. These results provide a local, mechanism-specific benchmark for value leakage in repeated private sensing and analytics.
tldr: This paper studies reconstruction limits for repeated differentially private aggregates using Cramér-Rao bounds, focusing on query geometry rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how repeated differentially private releases affect local reconstruction risk, beyond transcript length or cumulative privacy accounting.
method: Develops a nuisance-profiled Fisher geometry framework for Gaussian-calibrated repeated statistical queries, analyzing labeled-target and permutation-invariant releases.
result: Repeated copies of the same query provide only averaging gain; under zCDP/RDP accounting the risk is order-flat. For permutation-invariant releases, feature diversity determines identifiability.
conclusion: Release geometry determines local identifiability, while privacy accounting determines estimation precision; the work provides a benchmark for value leakage in private sensing.

title: Electromagnetic Characterization Of Magnetic Ring: Case Of Circular Cross-Section Shape
authors: Lars Sj\"oberg Taha El Hajji
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive two-dimensional analytical model of a toroidal magnetic ring with circular cross-section under sinusoidal excitation. Applying Maxwell's equations in local polar coordinates within a complex permeability, the model derives analytical expressions for the internal magnetic field, magnetic flux, complex impedance, and total losses. It rigorously separates the contributions of eddy current losses, hysteresis losses, and winding losses, while explicitly incorporating the skin effect in the conductive core via Bessel functions. An expression for the apparent permeability is also provided, enabling the nonlinear core behavior to be mapped onto simplified linear material models. The resulting analytical model offers a computationally efficient and accurate foundation for standardized magnetic material characterization, such as Brockhaus and Iwatsu ring measurements, as a powerful alternative to 2D and 3D finite element analysis.
tldr: This paper presents an analytical model for the electromagnetic characterization of a toroidal magnetic ring with circular cross-section, focusing on eddy current and hysteresis losses.
motivation: To provide a computationally efficient alternative to finite element analysis for standardized magnetic material characterization.
method: Maxwell's equations are solved in local polar coordinates with complex permeability, incorporating skin effect via Bessel functions.
result: Analytical expressions for internal magnetic field, flux, impedance, and losses are derived, including apparent permeability.
conclusion: The model offers an accurate and efficient tool for magnetic ring characterization, replacing 2D/3D FEM.

title: Design And Performance Of A Heated Gas Injector For Producing Cold Molecular Beams
authors: Avneesh Verma, Jack Mango, Shungo Fukaya, Arian Jadbabaie, Sepehr Ebadi, Ronald F. Garcia Ruiz, John M. Doyle
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We realize an injector device that supplies warm gas directly into a cryogenic environment. This injector has several advantageous features, including robustness, rigidity, simple installation, and excellent thermal isolation between a hot ([MATH]300 K) copper fill line and a cold ([MATH]3 K) cryogenic buffer gas cell. Less than 200 mW heat load on the cell is observed in realistic conditions of a molecular precision measurement experiment. A polyamide-imide (PAI) tube is the essential design feature. The fill line is epoxied to one end of the tube while the other end of the tube is connected to the cell via a slip-fit onto a brass nipple, realizing a complete vacuum-tight seal. PAI contracts on the brass nipple when cooled, forming a cryogenic leak-tight seal. The injector is easily (de-)mountable and rigid, with no significant displacement of the fill line relative to the cell observed during cooldown to 4 K. We characterize injector performance by flowing into the cell [MATH] through the hot fill line and cold [MATH] buffer gas through a separate cryogenic fill line while laser ablating a barium-containing target. This produces cold BaF free radicals, detected using absorption spectroscopy. This injector design will be employed to laser cool radium-containing molecules, such as [MATH] and [MATH], where leak-tight delivery of [MATH] and [MATH] reagents into a cryogenic buffer gas cell is required for scientific and safety reasons. These molecules are of particular interest for the study of symmetry-violating nuclear properties and searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.
tldr: This paper describes the design and performance of a heated gas injector for producing cold molecular beams, focusing on engineering aspects for precision measurement experiments.
motivation: To enable leak-tight delivery of reactive gases into a cryogenic buffer gas cell for producing cold molecules, which are used in searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.
method: The injector uses a polyamide-imide (PAI) tube to thermally isolate a hot fill line from a cold cell, with a slip-fit seal that becomes leak-tight upon cooling. Performance is characterized by flowing gas and laser ablation to produce BaF molecules, detected via absorption spectroscopy.
result: The injector achieves less than 200 mW heat load on the cell, is rigid and easy to mount, and maintains a vacuum-tight seal during cooldown to 4 K.
conclusion: The injector design is robust and suitable for delivering reactive chemicals for cold molecule production in precision measurement experiments.

title: Exact Propagating Dirac Wave Packets In An Attractive Coulomb-like Potential
authors: Siddhant Das
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct exact, positive-energy, normalizable wave-packet solutions of the Dirac equation in the axisymmetric potential [MATH] -- to our knowledge, the first such solutions in any external potential. Remarkably, one family comprises only elementary functions whose longitudinal profiles reproduce the free-Schr\"odinger Hermite--Gauss wave packets in the nonrelativistic limit. All packets share two striking features: (i) a probability density that is pointwise decoupled from spin orientation -- despite the inherent spin-orbit coupling of the Dirac equation -- and (ii) a complete freezing of their time evolution at the critical coupling [MATH]. We also present a simple scheme that maps solutions of the 2D Helmholtz equation to further exact Dirac wave packets.
tldr: Constructs exact Dirac wave packets in an attractive Coulomb-like potential, with decoupled probability density and frozen evolution at critical coupling.
motivation: To find exact, normalizable wave-packet solutions of the Dirac equation in an external potential, which are rare and important for understanding relativistic quantum dynamics.
method: Analytical construction using separation of variables and mapping to 2D Helmholtz equation; solutions expressed in terms of elementary functions and special functions.
result: Obtained two families of exact wave packets with pointwise spin-independent probability density and complete freezing of time evolution at a critical coupling strength.
conclusion: These exact solutions provide a new tool for studying relativistic quantum mechanics and may have implications for quantum information or thermodynamics, but the paper does not address those connections.

title: Deep Research In Physical Sciences: A Multi-Agent Framework And Comprehensive Benchmark
authors: Yigeng Jiang, Tengchao Yang, Taoyong Cui, Jiaxing Wan, Yuan Wang, Weida Wang, Zhiyu Liu, Chuyi Peng, Binzhao Luo, Maoli Gao, Huaihai Huang, Yuqianer Zeng, Ziyang Zheng, Dongchen Huang, Chao Chen, Zichao Liu, Weiping Shen, Shuchen Pu, Siyu Zhou, Runmin Ma, Yusong Hu, Fei Chao, Bo Zhang, Xiawu Zheng, Zifu Wang, Lei Bai, Yunqi Cai, Shufei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep research agents are Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems designed for autonomous, multi-step scientific reasoning, and they hold immense potential for accelerating research in the physical sciences. However, comprehensive and in-depth evaluations of their capabilities within this domain remain lacking. To address this gap, we introduce PhySciBench, a benchmark highly relevant to physical science research, comprising 200 expert-curated questions, balanced between physics and chemistry, across six task categories that reflect real-world scientific workflows. Evaluations of state-of-the-art models and agent systems on PhySciBench reveal limited performance; even the strongest baseline, Gemini Deep Research, achieves an accuracy of only 33.5%. Analysis of failure cases identifies three recurrent deficiencies: fragility in extended reasoning chains, limited knowledge transfer across steps, and a lack of physics-grounded self-verification. Motivated by these findings, we develop DelveAgent, a modular multi-agent framework equipped with an adaptive planning loop, dual-granularity memory, and a hierarchical physics-grounded reflection mechanism. Across four scientific benchmarks, DelveAgent improves accuracy by up to 7.5 percentage points while reducing inference costs to approximately one-third of the strongest baseline. These results establish the significance of PhySciBench as a critical benchmark for evaluating AI systems in the physical sciences and demonstrate that architectural specialization can effectively enhance the reliability of autonomous scientific research.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark and multi-agent framework for evaluating LLM-based research agents in physical sciences, with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: There is a lack of comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating AI systems in physical science research, and existing models show limited performance.
method: The authors create PhySciBench with 200 expert-curated questions and develop DelveAgent, a modular multi-agent framework with adaptive planning, dual-granularity memory, and physics-grounded reflection.
result: DelveAgent improves accuracy by up to 7.5 percentage points over baselines while reducing inference costs to about one-third.
conclusion: PhySciBench is a critical benchmark for AI in physical sciences, and architectural specialization enhances autonomous research reliability.

title: Magnetic-polarization-dependent Spectroscopy Of Lanthanide-doped Anisotropic Crystals
authors: Zoe Liestmann, Luca Koldeweyh, Moritz Badtke, Sascha Kalusniak, Christian Kr\"ankel, Hiroki Tanaka
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate that absorption and emission spectra of trivalent lanthanide-doped anisotropic crystals can exhibit a significant magnetic-polarization dependence, which has been largely overlooked in spectroscopic studies to date. Focusing on the uniaxial laser host LiYF4 (YLF) doped with Yb3+, Tm3+, Er3+, and Ho3+, we measure magnetic-polarization-dependent absorption and emission spectra for transitions with strong magnetic-dipole (MD) contributions predicted by theory. Our results reveal that MD-induced spectral anisotropy, i.e., spectral differences for the same electric field orientation but for different magnetic field orientations, is present even in these well-established laser materials. A complete spectroscopic characterization of uniaxial crystals requires three polarizations, including the [MATH]-polarization, with both the electric field vector E and the magnetic field vector H perpendicular to the c-axis (E [MATH] c, H [MATH] c), in addition to the commonly used two polarizations [MATH] (E [MATH] c, H [MATH] c) and [MATH] (E [MATH] c, H [MATH] c). We further discuss the observed MD-induced spectral anisotropy and calculated MD branching ratios, the impact of the anisotropy on emission cross-section calculations, and the relevance of our results to other uniaxial and biaxial crystals.
tldr: This paper studies magnetic-polarization-dependent spectroscopy of lanthanide-doped anisotropic crystals, focusing on spectral anisotropy due to magnetic-dipole transitions.
motivation: To highlight that magnetic-polarization effects are often overlooked in spectroscopy of uniaxial crystals, and to demonstrate that three polarizations are needed for complete characterization.
method: Experimental absorption and emission spectra measurements on YLF crystals doped with Yb3+, Tm3+, Er3+, and Ho3+ under different magnetic field orientations.
result: Significant magnetic-polarization-dependent spectral differences are observed for transitions with strong magnetic-dipole contributions, confirming theoretical predictions.
conclusion: A complete spectroscopic characterization of uniaxial crystals requires three polarizations, including the π-polarization with both E and H perpendicular to the c-axis.

title: A Skew Polynomial Framework For Constructing Division Algebras And Linear Maximum Rank Distance Codes
authors: Susanne Pumpluen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct division algebras and linear maximum rank distance (MRD) matrix codes using skew polynomials over fields. The non-unital division algebras we obtain generalize several prominent constructions: Sheekey's twisted cyclic pre-semifields, i.e. the pre-semifields associated with Jha-Johnson semifields and the semifields associated with Albert's generalized twisted fields. Our linear MRD codes generalize the constructions of Lobillo, Santonastaso and Sheekey. We present criteria for these algebras to be division algebras, respectively, for when these codes have maximum rank, and compare isotopic division algebras that appear throughout recent and classical literature. We compute some of their invariants.
tldr: This paper constructs division algebras and linear maximum rank distance codes using skew polynomials over fields, generalizing known constructions.
motivation: To unify and extend constructions of division algebras and MRD codes, which have applications in coding theory and cryptography.
method: Uses skew polynomial rings over fields to define non-unital division algebras and linear MRD codes, providing criteria for division algebra and maximum rank.
result: Generalizes Sheekey's twisted cyclic pre-semifields and Lobillo et al.'s MRD codes; computes invariants and compares isotopic algebras.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified approach to constructing division algebras and MRD codes, with potential for further generalizations.

title: Inferential Models: The Power Of Auxiliary Variables For Reasoning With Scientific Uncertainty
authors: Chuanhai Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central challenge in scientific inference is to produce uncertainty assessments that are both situation-specific and frequency-calibrated. This article examines inferential models (IMs) as a framework for prior-free probabilistic reasoning with scientific uncertainty. The central IM idea is to view the auxiliary variables in a sampling model as the source of model-based uncertainty. R. A. Fisher's fiducial inference transfers auxiliary randomness to the parameter space before applying probability calculus; IMs instead predict the unobserved auxiliary value with calibrated predictive random sets (PRSs) and transfer the resulting plausibility statements only afterward. This change in order yields valid uncertainty assessments and clarifies the relations among Fisherian fiducial reasoning, Neymanian confidence theory, Dempster-Shafer belief functions, generalized fiducial inference, and IMs. By comparing IMs with objective-prior Bayesian inference, the article argues that E. T. Jaynes' logic-of-science ambition can be continued without forcing all scientific uncertainty into a precise prior distribution because calibrated imprecision is often essential. Finally, the article suggests that a differential-geometric theory of IMs may be within reach, offering a possible route to foundational questions traditionally framed in terms of the likelihood principle.
tldr: This paper presents inferential models as a framework for prior-free probabilistic reasoning, focusing on auxiliary variables and calibrated predictive random sets.
motivation: To address the challenge of producing uncertainty assessments that are both situation-specific and frequency-calibrated without relying on prior distributions.
method: The paper develops inferential models (IMs) by predicting unobserved auxiliary values with calibrated predictive random sets and transferring plausibility statements to the parameter space.
result: IMs provide valid uncertainty assessments and clarify relationships among Fisherian fiducial inference, Neymanian confidence theory, Dempster-Shafer belief functions, and generalized fiducial inference.
conclusion: The IM framework offers a way to continue Jaynes' logic-of-science ambition without forcing all uncertainty into precise priors, and suggests a potential differential-geometric theory.

title: A Spectral Based Coefficient Of Determination For The Fit Of An MA(q) Model
authors: Sebastian K\"uhnert Holger Dette
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a spectral based coefficient of determination to measure how well the spectral density of a stationary process is represented by the class of MA([MATH]) models. Using periodogram-based estimators, we establish asymptotic normality, derive tests for the MA([MATH]) hypothesis, and construct procedures for determining the smallest order [MATH] achieving a prescribed approximation quality.
tldr: This paper develops a spectral-based coefficient of determination for assessing how well an MA(q) model fits a stationary time series.
motivation: To measure the approximation quality of MA(q) models for stationary processes using spectral density.
method: Uses periodogram-based estimators and establishes asymptotic normality to derive tests and order selection procedures.
result: Provides a coefficient of determination and hypothesis tests for the MA(q) assumption.
conclusion: The proposed method enables data-driven selection of the MA order with a prescribed approximation quality.

title: Computing Resonances Of Perturbed Schr\"odinger Equations: Application To Reissner-Norsdtr\"om-de Sitter Black Holes
authors: Genevi\`eve Dusson Valentin Arrigoni (UMLP)
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a numerical method for computing resonances of one-dimensional Schr\"odinger equations perturbed by a compactly supported potential, via finding zeros of the Wronskian associated with Jost solutions of the reference equation, computed through the resolution of Cauchy problems. All resonances located in a given domain are found efficiently using a defeated Newton algorithm. A key ingredient of the method is the choice of reference potential for which Jost solutions are known, which removes spurious resonances often encountered numerically. We test this method on three types of reference potentials and perturbations thereof: P\"oschl-Teller potentials, exponentially decaying potentials, and potentials associated with Reissner-Nordstr\"omde Sitter black holes. In particular we study the impact of perturbations on the resonances, and the stability of small resonances under perturbation. As an illustration, we use the method to numerically study the strong cosmic censorship hypothesis.
tldr: A numerical method for computing resonances of perturbed Schrödinger equations, applied to black hole physics.
motivation: To efficiently compute resonances of one-dimensional Schrödinger equations with compactly supported perturbations, avoiding spurious resonances.
method: Uses a defeated Newton algorithm to find zeros of the Wronskian of Jost solutions, with a carefully chosen reference potential.
result: Demonstrates the method on Pöschl-Teller, exponentially decaying, and Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole potentials, studying resonance stability.
conclusion: The method is effective for computing resonances and can be used to study the strong cosmic censorship hypothesis.

title: Exponential Ergodicity Of Exact And Numerical Solutions For McKean-Vlasov SDEs Driven By L\'evy Noise
authors: Yang Sun, Yuhang Zhang, Minghui Song
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the exponential ergodicity of the exact solution and the tamed Euler solution for McKean-Vlasov stochastic differential equations driven by L\'evy noise. First, we establish exponential ergodicity for both the original equation and the tamed Euler method. Then we prove the convergence of the numerical invariant measure to the exact invariant measure, which is obtained by combining the propagation of chaos (PoC) result with the strong convergence of the tamed Euler scheme. Furthermore, we derive a convergence rate for the numerical invariant measure by establishing uniform-in-time PoC and uniform-in-time convergence of the tamed Euler method. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the theoretical results.
tldr: This paper studies exponential ergodicity of McKean-Vlasov SDEs with Lévy noise and their numerical approximations.
motivation: Understanding ergodicity of McKean-Vlasov SDEs is important for mean-field models, but the paper focuses on stochastic analysis rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors prove exponential ergodicity for the exact solution and a tamed Euler scheme, then combine propagation of chaos with strong convergence to analyze numerical invariant measures.
result: Exponential ergodicity is established for both exact and numerical solutions, and convergence rates for the numerical invariant measure are derived.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical guarantees for simulating McKean-Vlasov SDEs with Lévy noise, but has no connection to the user's research interests.

title: Sub-optimal Control By Primal-dual Gradient Dynamics
authors: Arjan van der Schaft
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note generalizes the port-Hamiltonian formulation of the continuous time primal-dual gradient algorithm for static constrained convex optimization to the convex optimal control problem.The resulting dynamics is shown to be a port-Hamiltonian system of partial differential equations, involving ordinary physical time as well 'algorithmic' time. Convergence to the optimal control solution is indicated, and it is argued that sub-optimal control strategies could be derived starting from the partial differential equation formulation.
tldr: This paper generalizes the port-Hamiltonian formulation of primal-dual gradient dynamics to convex optimal control, resulting in a PDE system that converges to the optimal solution.
motivation: To extend the continuous-time primal-dual gradient algorithm from static optimization to optimal control problems, enabling sub-optimal control strategies.
method: The authors formulate the optimal control problem as a port-Hamiltonian system of PDEs, combining physical time and algorithmic time, and analyze convergence.
result: The resulting dynamics is a port-Hamiltonian PDE system that converges to the optimal control solution, and sub-optimal strategies can be derived from the PDE formulation.
conclusion: The port-Hamiltonian framework provides a unified approach for primal-dual dynamics in optimal control, with potential for sub-optimal control design.

title: Probabilistic Representation And Classical Solutions Of Wave Equations With Complex Polynomial Nonlinearities
authors: Nicolas Privault Joshua J. Y. Chan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We review the probabilistic representation of solutions of wave equations with polynomial nonlinearities in spatial dimensions d=1,2,3 using stochastic branching processes. Under regularity assumptions on the initial data, we derive conditions ensuring the integrability of the corresponding Monte Carlo estimator, and the existence and smoothness of mild and classical solutions. We also present numerical results and comparisons with grid-based algorithms for the solution of nonlinear wave equations.
tldr: This paper uses probabilistic branching processes to represent and solve nonlinear wave equations with polynomial nonlinearities in low dimensions.
motivation: To provide a probabilistic representation for classical solutions of nonlinear wave equations, enabling Monte Carlo simulation and existence proofs.
method: Stochastic branching processes are used to represent solutions, with conditions derived for integrability of Monte Carlo estimators and smoothness of solutions.
result: Conditions for existence and smoothness of mild and classical solutions are established, and numerical comparisons with grid-based algorithms are presented.
conclusion: The probabilistic approach offers an alternative method for solving nonlinear wave equations, with potential advantages in certain regimes.

title: On The Ascent And The Angle Between The Null Space And The Range Of Elementary Operators
authors: Janko Bra\v{c}i\v{c}, Bojan Kuzma, Hranislav Stankovi\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2606.18930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the angle between the null space and the range of elementary operators of length one or two acting on [MATH], the Banach algebra of all bounded linear operators on a complex Banach space [MATH]. For the multiplication operator [MATH], we characterize positivity of this angle in terms of the corresponding angles for [MATH] and [MATH]. For elementary operators of length two [MATH], we establish conditions under which the angle is positive, and the ascent of [MATH] equals one. Finally, for a generalized derivation [MATH] and an injective holomorphic function [MATH] on a neighborhood of [MATH], we show that the angle between the null space and the range of [MATH] is positive whenever the angle between the null space and the range of [MATH] is positive.
tldr: This paper studies the angle between the null space and the range of elementary operators on Banach algebras, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize positivity of the angle and ascent for certain elementary operators, which is a purely mathematical problem in operator theory.
method: They use functional analysis techniques to analyze multiplication operators, elementary operators of length two, and generalized derivations.
result: They establish conditions for positive angle and ascent equal to one for these operators, and relate the angle of a generalized derivation to that of its argument.
conclusion: The work contributes to operator theory but has no apparent application to the user's research interests.

title: Optimal Score Function Estimation Via Derivatives Constraints
authors: Thomas Bonis, Thanh Mai Pham Ngoc, Viet Chi Tran
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of score function estimation via empirical risk minimization. We first start with the question of inferring the score function of a probability measure [MATH] with density on the flat torus from a sample of distribution [MATH]. We show that constraining the hypothesis space to a Sobolev ball is sufficient to prevent overfitting and obtaining minimax estimation rates. We then consider the problem of score function estimation in the context of score-based generative modeling. Again, under a conjecture tying the score estimation rates to the quality of the output of a score-based generative model, we obtain minimax rates for such an approach using score function estimators obtained by constraining the hypothesis class to a Sobolev ball.
